fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to his life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the mind and heart of Jonathan Edwards — the sovereignty and the beauty of God, true religion as holy affections, and the end for which God created the world: His own glory, delighted in by His creatures. Eighteen short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as a companion to Edwards's own public-domain works, which readers are warmly encouraged to go to directly.
fields.about_html:
This is a companion to Jonathan Edwards, not a book by him. Written by Ochorus, it distils the thought of America's greatest theologian into eighteen short chapters an ordinary reader can carry.

Edwards saw further into the greatness and beauty of God than almost anyone who has written in English, and he bent the whole force of a formidable mind to a single end: that God might be seen as supremely glorious and enjoyed as supremely good. This volume traces that vision through his most important works — the sovereignty of God, the beauty of holiness, true religion as holy affections, the end for which God created the world — and through the sterner texts, like the sermon on sinners in the hands of an angry God, that people remember and misremember. Each chapter closes in questions and a prayer, because Edwards held that truth unfelt and unobeyed has not yet been truly known.

Edwards's own writings are in the public domain and freely available, and this companion names them throughout so the reader may go to the source. It quotes Scripture from the Authorised (King James) Version, the Bible Edwards preached from, and is offered only to open the door to the man's own pages.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light. PSALM 36:9

Most people who know the name Jonathan Edwards know one thing about him, and the one thing is misleading. They know that he preached a sermon about sinners dangling like spiders over a fire. It appears in school anthologies as a specimen of Puritan severity, and it has fixed his reputation for two centuries as a grim man who frightened people for a living. The sermon is real. He did preach it, at Enfield in July 1741, and we shall come to it. But it is one sermon out of roughly twelve hundred that survive, and it is thoroughly unrepresentative of the rest. The man who preached it also wrote that heaven is a world of love, that God’s purpose in creating anything at all was the overflow of His own fullness, and that the difference between a true Christian and a false one is finally a matter of what the soul finds beautiful. He was, in the plainest terms, a theologian of joy who happened once to write something unforgettable about hell.

Why he still matters

Edwards has a strange standing. He is widely agreed to be the most powerful mind the American church has produced, and he is very little read. His treatises are difficult; his sentences are long; his categories belong to the eighteenth century. Most believers who admire him have got him at second hand. That is a pity, because his central concern is not eighteenth-century at all. He spent his life on a single question, and it is the question the church in every age is least able to answer honestly: how do you tell the difference between a person who has been changed by God and a person who has merely been stirred? He asked it because he had to. He stood at the centre of two great awakenings, watched thousands profess conversion, watched a proportion of them fall away, and refused to draw either of the easy conclusions — that the whole thing was delusion, or that every emotional response was the Spirit of God. He insisted on a third possibility that requires far more work: that God was genuinely at work, that counterfeit was genuinely present, and that the two could be distinguished.

Any church that has ever run a crusade, counted decisions, or wondered what became of last year’s converts is standing where Edwards stood.

How this book is arranged

Eighteen short chapters set out the teaching for which Edwards is chiefly remembered, beginning where he began — with God — and moving outward through sin, salvation, the affections, revival, love, and finally prayer and the hope of what God intends to do in history. Each chapter ends in the same two places: a set of application points and a prayer. This is deliberate, and Edwards would have approved. He held with great firmness that knowledge which never reaches practice is not saving knowledge at all. The last and longest sign in his Religious Affections is Christian practice — how a man actually lives — and he ranked it above every inward experience a person might report. A chapter of this book that is read and admired but not obeyed has, by its own argument, failed. Read one chapter a day, or one a week. Stop at the application points. Pray the prayer, or better, pray your own. Throughout, his own sermons and treatises are named, so the reader may follow any thread back to its source. A short guide to his works is provided at the end. Edwards’s writings are out of copyright and widely available at no cost, which means that unlike most great theologians he can be read entire by anyone with an internet connection and some patience.

One more thing must be said at the outset, and it is better said plainly. This is not a book of hero-worship. Jonathan Edwards owned slaves. He purchased a girl named Venus in Newport in 1731, when she was about fourteen. Over the following years his household included others — Leah, Titus, Joseph, Sue, Rose. He opposed the Atlantic slave trade and wrote against it, he baptised black believers and received them into full membership of his church when other ministers would not, and he recorded in his notebooks that master and servant have one Maker who made them alike with the same nature. And he defended the institution itself in a draft letter, and he died without freeing anyone. There is no way to soften this, and it should not be softened. It was not a blind spot of an age that knew no better; men in his own colony were arguing against slavery in his lifetime, and he answered them. The people who worked in his house made possible the study that produced the books we still read. That fact belongs in any honest account of him. Why then read him at all? For the same reason we read David, who arranged a murder, and Peter, who denied his Lord, and Paul, who held the coats. The Scriptures themselves record the failures of the men God used, and they do it without embarrassment and without excusing anything. God has never had any material to work with but sinners, and He has never pretended otherwise. There is also a grim irony that Edwards himself would have understood. Within a generation, his own son and his closest theological heir, Samuel Hopkins, became leading opponents of slavery — and they argued their case directly from his theology, insisting they were only carrying his own principles where he had failed to carry them. His doctrine of true virtue, of benevolence extended to all being, turned out to contain the refutation of his own practice. That is precisely what he taught us to expect. No teaching was more central to him than that the human heart is deceitful beyond our capacity to detect, that we are most blind where we most benefit, and that even a converted man may harbour what he has never examined. A book presenting Edwards as a spotless saint would be contradicting the very doctrine it was written to commend. So the counsel of this book is the counsel of Scripture: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Weigh every chapter against the Word of God. Where Edwards is faithful to Scripture — and on the glory of God, the necessity of the new birth, the testing of religious experience and the beauty of holiness, he is faithful indeed — receive it gladly and act upon it. Where he was wrong, and he was, learn from that too. It is one of the more useful lessons he has to teach.

A final word about the reader this book assumes. Edwards wrote for an English-speaking colonial congregation of farmers and tradesmen in a river valley in Massachusetts. He is now read across the world — in Korea, in Brazil, in Nigeria, in China — by Christians whose circumstances share nothing with his. The reason is not that his setting travels well. It plainly does not. It is that he dealt almost entirely with what does not vary: what God is like, what the human heart is like, and how a person may know whether the grace of God has actually touched him. Those questions are already waiting wherever this book is opened, in whatever language it is carried.

fields.title: A Life Spent for the Glory of God
fields.body_html:
Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. PSALM 73:25

A house full of daughters. Jonathan Edwards was born on the fifth of October, 1703, in East Windsor, Connecticut, a frontier parish beside the Connecticut River. He was the fifth of eleven children and the only son; his ten sisters were all unusually tall, and their father was said to joke that he had sixty feet of daughters. His father, Timothy Edwards, was the parish minister, a Harvard man who supplemented a modest salary by farming and by tutoring boys for college. His mother, Esther, was the daughter of Solomon Stoddard, the formidable minister of Northampton, thirty-five miles upriver — a man so dominant in the Connecticut Valley that he was known as the Pope of the region. Between father and grandfather, the boy was surrounded by ministry from birth. He was extraordinarily quick. As a child he wrote observations on the flying spiders of the New England woods, with a precision that would not embarrass a naturalist. He entered the Collegiate School — soon to be Yale — in 1716, not yet thirteen years old, and graduated at the head of his class in 1720. He stayed two further years in New Haven studying divinity.

A new sense of things. The intellect came early. The religion took longer, and he was honest about why. By his own later account in the Personal Narrative, he had been religious from boyhood — he built a booth in a swamp to pray in, he had seasons of great fervour — and none of it had touched the thing that needed touching. What he could not accept was the sovereignty of God. The doctrine that God chooses whom He will save appeared to him horrible. He fought it for years. Then, sometime in 1721, reading a verse he had read a hundred times before — Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever (1 Timothy 1:17) — something opened. He described a sense of the glory of the divine being diffusing itself through his soul, a kind of sweetness altogether new, and quite unlike anything he had experienced in religion before. What is significant is what changed. The doctrine he had hated did not become easier to accept; it became beautiful. He found himself delighting in the very thing that had offended him. This experience became the seed of nearly all his later theology: the conviction that conversion is not the mind being persuaded but the heart being given a new taste, a new sense, so that what was repellent becomes lovely. Around this time he began his Diary and his seventy Resolutions — a young man’s programme for a life wholly ordered towards God, reviewed weekly, and shot through with an urgency about time that never left him.

Northampton. After a brief pastorate in New York and two years as a tutor at Yale, he was called in 1726 to assist his grandfather at Northampton. In July 1727 he married Sarah Pierpont, whom he had first noticed at thirteen and described in a famous scrap of writing as a young woman who walked about singing, beloved of that Great Being who made the world. The marriage was, by every account, unusually happy. They had eleven children. Solomon Stoddard died in 1729 and Edwards inherited the largest and most influential pulpit outside Boston. He kept a punishing schedule — thirteen hours a day in the study by some accounts — and preached to a congregation that had grown accustomed to revivals and to being told they were the finest church in the valley. In 1731 he was invited to preach in Boston, and chose to tell the assembled ministers that God is most glorified in the total dependence of man upon Him. It made his name. Then, in the winter of 1734 and into 1735, something happened in Northampton that neither he nor anyone else had arranged. Following a series of sermons on justification by faith alone, the town was seized. Conversions ran into the hundreds; the character of the place visibly altered. Edwards wrote it up carefully and without exaggeration, and A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God was published in London in 1737. It made him famous across the Atlantic, and it supplied the template by which a generation would recognise revival.

The Great Awakening. The larger wave came at the end of the decade. George Whitefield preached at Northampton in October 1740 — Edwards is said to have wept through the sermon — and the colonies caught fire. On the eighth of July 1741, at Enfield, Edwards preached Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God. Accounts describe the congregation crying out before he had finished. He read it, as he read most of his sermons, in a level voice from a manuscript held close to his eyes. But the awakening also produced disorder — shrieking, visions, itinerants denouncing settled ministers, and confident claims to direct revelation. The churches divided between those who declared the whole movement a work of God and those who declared it a delirium. Edwards took the harder path, and it cost him friends on both sides. In The Distinguishing Marks of a Work of the Spirit of God (1741) and Some Thoughts Concerning the Present Revival (1742) he argued that a genuine work of God may be accompanied by human excess without ceasing to be genuine, and that the way to judge is not by the noise but by the fruit. The mature statement came in 1746. A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections is his masterpiece, and it is a hard book, because it takes away every comfortable test a person might apply to himself and replaces them with ones that cannot be faked.

Dismissal. His grandfather had admitted to the Lord’s Table anyone of upright life, whether or not they professed conversion. Edwards came to believe this was wrong, and said so. The controversy consumed two years and destroyed his ministry. On the twenty-second of June, 1750, the congregation voted to dismiss him, by something like two hundred and thirty votes to twenty-three. He was forty-six, with a large family and no income. His farewell sermon is remarkably free of bitterness. He told them he would meet them again at the judgment seat, and left it there.

Stockbridge, and the end. In 1751 he took the only position available: a frontier settlement at Stockbridge, with a handful of English families and a mission to the Mahican and Mohawk people. He learned to preach through an interpreter, in short plain sermons, and defended the mission against the settlers who were defrauding it. It should have been an exile. It became the most productive period of his life. In seven years at the edge of the wilderness, in a house crowded with children and interrupted by war, he wrote Freedom of the Will (1754), The Great Christian Doctrine of Original Sin Defended, The Nature of True Virtue and The End for Which God Created the World. In 1757 the College of New Jersey — later Princeton — invited him to be its president, following the death of his son-in-law. He protested that he was unfit, awkward in company, and better suited to a study. He went anyway. He arrived in February 1758. Smallpox was in the town, and he was inoculated, which was then a genuine risk. The inoculation went wrong. He died on the twenty-second of March, 1758, aged fifty-four, having been president for about five weeks. He was conscious near the end, and left a message for his absent wife about the uncommon union between them and his hope that it would continue for ever. To those around the bed he said that they should trust in God, and then they need not fear. Sarah died six months later. On hearing of his death she wrote that God had made her adore His goodness — that He had given them her husband for so long, and that she and her children were left to God.

fields.title: The End for Which God Created the World
fields.body_html:
For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen. ROMANS 11:36

Everything in Jonathan Edwards begins here, and nothing in him can be understood without it. In the last years of his life, in a crowded house on the Massachusetts frontier, he wrote a dissertation asking a question most people never think to ask. Not how did God make the world, nor when, but why. What was God after? What did He intend to accomplish by there being anything at all?

An answer we find uncomfortable

Edwards answered that God’s ultimate end in creating the world was the glory of God — His own fullness known, communicated, esteemed and enjoyed. That answer has always troubled people, and it troubles modern readers most of all. It sounds like vanity. We do not admire human beings who arrange everything for their own praise, and we instinctively resist a God who appears to do the same. Edwards took the objection seriously, and his reply is one of the most bracing arguments in Christian theology. It runs like this. For any being to value something above what is most valuable would be a falsehood — an error about reality. If God is in fact the highest good, the source and standard of every excellence, then for God to esteem anything else more highly than Himself would not be humility. It would be a lie. It would be God preferring the lesser to the greater, which is precisely what we call sin when we do it. So God’s regard for His own glory is not self-obsession. It is simply God seeing accurately.

I am the Lord: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another. ISAIAH 42:8

Why this is good news and not bad

But Edwards pressed further, and this is where the doctrine turns from intimidating to glorious. Suppose God is the highest good. Then the best possible thing that could happen to a creature is to receive God — to know Him, see Him, love Him and enjoy Him. There is no superior gift available anywhere in the universe, because there is nothing superior to God. Which means that when God acts to display His own glory, He is not competing with our happiness. He is securing it. The two are the same act.

Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore. PSALM 16:11

A God who sought our happiness instead of His glory would have to offer us something less than Himself, and would therefore be offering us something less than the best. Only a God who is thoroughly committed to His own glory can give His creatures what they most need, because what they most need is Him. Edwards described the whole arrangement as an emanation and a returning — the fullness of God flowing out into the creation, and then flowing back to Him in the knowledge, love and joy of creatures who have received it. The universe is not a machine God built. It is an overflow.

Where Scripture puts the accent

He built the case not on philosophy but on the sheer accumulation of biblical statements, and the accumulation is impressive once you begin to look.

Even every one that is called by my name: for I have created him for my glory, I have formed him; yea, I have made him. ISAIAH 43:7
For mine own sake, even for mine own sake, will I do it …and I will not give my glory unto another. ISAIAH 48:11

Election is to the praise of the glory of his grace (Ephesians 1:6). Creation is by him, and for him (Colossians 1:16). Redemption issues in a doxology; providence issues in a doxology; the last book of the Bible is one long doxology. Even eating and drinking are brought under the same end: whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). Edwards’s point was that this is not one theme among many in Scripture. It is the theme under all the others, and once a reader sees it he cannot stop seeing it.

What it does to a life

The practical consequence is a reordering of the whole self, and it is more searching than it first appears.

fields.body_html:
That no flesh should glory in his presence …He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:29, 31

In July 1731, a young minister from a country parish was invited to preach the public lecture in Boston before the assembled clergy of New England. It was the most prestigious pulpit available to him, and he was twenty-seven years old. He chose to tell them that they contributed nothing. The sermon was published as God Glorified in the Work of Redemption, by the Greatness of Man’s Dependence upon Him, in the Whole of It. It was Edwards’s first appearance in print, and it announced the theme he would spend the rest of his life developing.

The three prepositions

His structure came from the text itself, and it is worth following closely, because it is not merely tidy — it is exhaustive. The redeemed have all their good of God. He is the first cause, the fountain from which everything proceeds. Nothing we possess originated with us.

For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it? 1 CORINTHIANS 4:7

The redeemed have all their good through God. He is not only the source but the means. Salvation does not come to us by some channel God set up and then left running; it comes through the Son who purchased it and the Spirit who applies it. God does not merely supply the materials of our salvation; He is the medium of it at every point. And the redeemed have all their good in God. This is the part most readily forgotten. God does not give us a happiness that is separable from Himself, some blessing we could carry away and enjoy at a distance. The good He gives is Himself. Heaven is not a reward located near God; heaven is God. Of Him, through Him, in Him. Edwards’s conclusion was blunt: at no point in the entire transaction does the creature have anything to contribute, and therefore at no point does the creature have anything to boast about.

Grace does not reduce dependence — it deepens it

Here Edwards made an observation that overturns a common assumption. We tend to think of grace as a kind of assistance — God supplying what we lack so that we can then manage. On that view, the more grace we receive, the less dependent we become, rather as a child needs less help as he grows. Edwards argued the reverse. The redeemed are more dependent on God than unfallen Adam was, not less. Adam depended on God for his existence and his faculties. The redeemed sinner depends on God for those things and also for his righteousness, which is not his own; for his faith, which is a gift; for his perseverance, which is kept by another; and for his final glory, which is wholly of grace. Redemption therefore magnifies dependence. That, in Edwards’s view, is exactly why God arranged salvation this way. The design was not merely to rescue sinners but to rescue them in a manner that made the rescuer’s glory unmistakable.

Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us. TITUS 3:5

The abolition of comparison

The pastoral consequence is enormous, and it is one of the most freeing things in Edwards. If everything I have was given, then comparison becomes meaningless. I cannot be superior to another believer on the basis of gifts I did not generate, any more than a man can be proud of the size of an inheritance he did nothing to earn. Paul’s question — who maketh thee to differ? — is designed to end the conversation before it begins. This cuts in both directions, and the second is the one we notice less. Comparison downward produces pride; comparison upward produces envy and despair. Both rest on the same error — the assumption that what we have is ours. Remove the assumption and both collapse together.

For without me ye can do nothing. JOHN 15:5

Edwards took nothing at full strength. Not a little. Not less than we might. Nothing.

There is a test buried in this doctrine, and it is uncomfortable. A man who truly believes he contributes nothing will not be devastated when he is overlooked, because he was never trading on his own account. He will not be inflated when he is praised, because he knows where the goods came from. His equilibrium under both flattery and neglect is the most reliable public evidence that the doctrine has got past his intellect and into his bones.

Prayer as the confession of dependence

If the doctrine of this chapter is true, then prayer is not principally a technique for obtaining things. It is the posture in which a creature acknowledges what he actually is. Edwards made this connection repeatedly, and it explains something otherwise puzzling. If God knows our needs before we ask, and intends to supply them, why ask at all? The answer is that God is not merely giving us things. He is drawing us into a relationship in which we know where everything comes from. A gift received without asking can be enjoyed without reference to the giver; a gift asked for and granted cannot. Prayer is how God arranges that His provision shall also be His self-revelation.

Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you. MATTHEW 7:7

There is a diagnostic in this, and it is uncomfortable. A prayerless Christian is not merely neglecting a duty. He is making a statement about his own self-sufficiency, whatever his theology says. We pray in proportion to our conscious need, which is why prayer collapses in prosperity and revives in crisis — and why crisis is so often a mercy. Edwards observed that the same principle governs how God distributes His blessings over time. He gives daily rather than in bulk, as He gave manna in the wilderness, so that dependence is renewed each morning rather than settled once. We would greatly prefer a lump sum. He gives us a day at a time, and calls it our daily bread.

Give us this day our daily bread. MATTHEW 6:11

This also reframes what we should be asking for. If our highest good is God Himself, then the most important prayers are not for circumstances but for Him — for more of His presence, a clearer sight of Christ, a heart that wants Him. Edwards noticed that such prayers are the ones we make least often, and the only ones we can be certain are according to His will.

If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him? LUKE 11:13
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. List three things you are quietly proud of. Trace each one back to where it came from, honestly, and see whether anything is left to boast in. 2. Notice this week when you compare yourself with another believer. Each time, answer Paul’s question: who made you to differ? 3. Watch your reaction to being overlooked. Do not suppress it — examine it. What does it reveal about what you thought was yours? 4. Thank God specifically for one ability you have always assumed was simply your own. 5. In prayer, ask not only for God’s help but for God Himself. Notice whether that is a strange request for you.

A PRAYER
Father, I have received everything and behaved as though I had earned something.
You are the fountain of all my good, the way by which it reaches me, and the good itself. There is nothing in my hands that You did not put there.
Deliver me from comparison — from the pride that looks down and the envy that looks up. Both are unbelief about where my life came from.
Make me content to be a receiver. And when I am overlooked, let me be steady, because I was never living on my own credit. Amen.

fields.title: The Sovereignty of God
fields.body_html:
But our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased. PSALM 115:3

Edwards did not arrive at the sovereignty of God as an inherited opinion. He arrived at it after years of resisting it, and the record of that resistance is one of the most valuable things he left us.

A doctrine he hated

In the Personal Narrative he describes his younger self’s objection with startling candour. The teaching that God chooses whom He will save and passes by others appeared to him horrible. He could not make it fit with anything he wanted to believe about God, and he argued against it in his own mind for a long time. Then something changed, and he was careful to describe the change accurately. He did not say that he found a knockdown argument. He said that the doctrine came to appear to him exceedingly pleasant, bright and sweet — that he came to delight in the absolute sovereignty of God. That sequence is important, and it recurs throughout his theology. The resolution was not intellectual capitulation. It was a change in what he found beautiful. He began to want a God like that. Any reader wrestling with these doctrines should note the pattern. Argument has its place, and Edwards was a formidable arguer. But he did not believe anyone was ever finally reconciled to the sovereignty of God by being out-reasoned. Something has to happen to the taste.

What Scripture claims

The claim itself is not obscure. It is stated repeatedly and without qualification.

And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou? DANIEL 4:35
For he saith to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy …So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. ROMANS 9:15–16

Edwards preached on these texts directly, notably in God’s Sovereignty in the Salvation of Men. His handling of the standard objection is characteristically severe and characteristically clarifying. The objection is that this is unfair. Edwards’s answer is that the objection misunderstands what is owed. Justice would give every sinner condemnation; nobody receives worse than justice. Mercy, by definition, is not owed to anyone — the moment it is owed it has stopped being mercy and become wages. God wrongs no one by giving some what none deserve.

Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus? ROMANS 9:20

He was aware this does not remove the difficulty from the heart. He did not pretend it did. What he insisted upon was that the difficulty is not an injustice in God but an offence to our sense of entitlement — and that our sense of entitlement is itself part of what needs saving.

Why it is a pastoral doctrine

It would be a mistake to file this under abstract theology. For Edwards it was intensely practical, and in two directions. It kills despair. If salvation depended on the sinner’s capacity to generate faith, then the hardened, the addicted, the long-resistant and the intellectually proud would be beyond hope, because they cannot. But if God is sovereign in salvation, no one is beyond reach. Edwards prayed for the most unlikely people in his parish with real expectation, precisely because the outcome did not depend on them. And it kills presumption. If God’s mercy is free, it cannot be commanded, scheduled or taken for granted. The man who assumes he can repent at a convenient time has misunderstood what repentance is and who grants it.

Seek ye the Lord while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near. ISAIAH 55:6

One caution, which Edwards’s own practice supplies better than any argument. Nobody preached God’s sovereignty more insistently, and nobody pleaded with sinners more urgently. He saw no tension whatever between the two, and he would have regarded a man who used divine sovereignty as a reason not to evangelise as having failed to understand it. The same Scripture that declares God’s absolute freedom in mercy commands us without qualification to call everyone.

Whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely. REVELATION 22:17

Hold both. Edwards did, all his life, and he never showed the slightest anxiety about it.

Sovereignty in providence

Edwards did not confine this doctrine to the question of who is saved. He applied it to everything that happens, and it was in the ordinary disasters of his own life that he had to prove whether he believed it. Scripture’s boldest statements on the subject concern the worst event in history. Peter tells the Jerusalem crowd that they took Jesus and crucified Him — genuinely guilty, genuinely responsible — and in the same breath that this happened by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23). The church at prayer says the same thing more explicitly still.

For of a truth against thy holy child Jesus …both Herod, and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles, and the people of Israel, were gathered together, for to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done. ACTS 4:27–28

The murder of the Son of God was the freely chosen wickedness of specific men, and it was the settled plan of God for the salvation of the world. Scripture asserts both without embarrassment, and Edwards took that as the pattern for every lesser instance.

But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive. GENESIS 50:20

Joseph does not say his brothers meant one thing and it happened to work out. He says God meant it — the same act, two intentions, one wicked and one good. Edwards had occasion to apply this. He was dismissed at forty-six from the most influential pulpit in the region, by his own congregation, after twenty-three years, with ten children still at home and no income. His letters from that period show a man genuinely wounded and genuinely settled. He went to a frontier village, and there wrote the four books on which his reputation now chiefly rests. Had he remained at Northampton, with its committees and its constant demands, it is unlikely he would have written any of them. He did not know that at the time. Nobody does.

And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose. ROMANS 8:28

fields.body_html:
Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven. MATTHEW 16:17

In 1734, before the revival that would make him famous, Edwards preached a sermon at Northampton whose title states its whole argument: A Divine and Supernatural Light, Immediately Imparted to the Soul by the Spirit of God, Shown to be both a Scriptural and Rational Doctrine. It is the hinge of his theology of conversion, and it answers a question that troubles thoughtful believers everywhere. How can two people hear the same sermon, read the same verse, receive the same information — and one be transformed while the other is merely informed?

What the light is not

Edwards was careful to fence the doctrine before building it, because he knew where enthusiasts would take it. This light is not new revelation. It does not add doctrines to Scripture, supply information not contained there, or grant impressions that carry the authority of the Word. Edwards was severe about that, and grew more severe as the awakening produced men claiming direct messages from heaven. Nor is it a vision, a voice, a feeling of excitement, or a sudden rush of emotion. Nor is it merely being deeply moved by a sermon — an experience available to anyone with a working imagination and a good preacher. What is it, then? A real sense of the divine excellency of the things already revealed in Scripture. Not new content. New perception of old content.

Knowing about, and knowing

His illustration is the one everybody remembers, and it is perfect. There is a difference, he said, between knowing that honey is sweet and tasting its sweetness. A man may have read every treatise on honey ever written. He may be able to describe its chemistry, its colour, its use in cookery, and give a lecture that would satisfy an examiner. And if he has never had honey on his tongue, there is something he does not know — something the lecture cannot supply and the taste conveys instantly.

O taste and see that the Lord is good. PSALM 34:8

Edwards called this the sense of the heart, and distinguished it sharply from what he called notional understanding. Notional understanding grasps the proposition. The sense of the heart apprehends the loveliness of what the proposition describes. A person may hold, correctly and sincerely, that God is holy, that Christ died for sinners, that grace is free. He may defend these against objection. And he may never once have seen them as beautiful. When he does — when the excellency of the thing lands on him — everything changes, and he cannot afterwards explain why he did not see it before.

For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:6

Note the language: light. The same God who spoke at creation speaks again, and the result is not additional information but illumination.

Why it must be given

It follows that no one can produce this in himself or in anyone else.

But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned. 1 CORINTHIANS 2:14

The difficulty is not that the natural man lacks intelligence. Edwards was emphatic on this, and it matters: a very clever person may be entirely blind here, and a very simple one may see clearly. The faculty required is not mental capacity. It is a spiritual taste that must be created. This is why Peter’s confession drew the response it did. He had said what others could have said. What the Lord commended was the source: flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee. Edwards would not let his hearers conclude that they should therefore sit passively and wait. God ordinarily gives this light through the means He has appointed — the reading and preaching of His Word. The farmer cannot make the rain, and he plants anyway.

The test of it

How does a person know whether he has this light or is deceiving himself?

Edwards gave a test that is impossible to counterfeit: the light produces love for the thing seen. A man who has genuinely perceived the excellency of God does not merely assent to God’s holiness; he finds it lovely, and he wants it in himself. The perception and the affection arrive together, because seeing beauty and loving it are one act. If a person’s religion consists of correct opinions that leave the heart unmoved and the life unaltered, he has notions, not light.

There is enormous comfort in this doctrine for those who feel their understanding is small. You are not required to be brilliant. Some of the people Edwards observed most transformed in the Northampton revival were servants, children and the uneducated, who grasped the loveliness of Christ while learned men debated at a distance. The light is not distributed according to intellect. It is given. Which means the right response to a passage of Scripture that has never moved you is not to study harder — though study — but to ask.

The means God uses

If this light is given and cannot be produced, does a believer simply wait? Edwards answered no, and his reasoning matters, because his doctrine has often been distorted into passivity. God ordinarily gives this light through means, and the chief means is His Word — read, preached, discussed and thought about. The Spirit does not usually illuminate a mind that has been given nothing to illuminate. Revelation is not an alternative to knowing the content of Scripture; it is the content becoming luminous.

So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. ROMANS 10:17

He put considerable weight on this in his preaching practice. His sermons are densely doctrinal, and deliberately so. He believed the preacher’s task was to set the truth before the mind as clearly and fully as possible — and then to press it upon the affections — while knowing perfectly well that neither the clarity nor the pressing could produce the light. The farmer’s position is exactly analogous. He cannot make it rain. He ploughs anyway, because rain falls on ploughed and unploughed ground alike and only one of them yields a harvest.

I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase. 1 CORINTHIANS 3:6

This also explains why doctrine matters so much to a theologian of the affections, which surprises some readers. You cannot find beautiful what you do not know. A person with a thin, vague, sentimental idea of God has very little for the Spirit to make lovely. The richer and more accurate a believer’s grasp of who God is and what He has done, the more surface there is for the light to strike. So Edwards’s counsel to anyone who finds Scripture dull is twofold, and both halves are necessary. Study — learn the content, understand the argument, know what the passage actually says. And ask — because all the study in the world will not, of itself, produce a taste for what is there.

Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures. LUKE 24:45

Those disciples had walked with Him for three years and heard the Scriptures all their lives. They still needed their understanding opened, and He opened it.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Before reading Scripture this week, ask specifically to see the beauty of what you read, not merely to understand it. 2. Identify one doctrine you believe correctly and have never found lovely. Bring exactly that one to God and ask for light on it. 3. Test yourself with Edwards’s test: does what you know about God produce love for God? Answer honestly rather than quickly. 4. Refuse to substitute strong feeling for spiritual sight. Ask whether a moving experience left you loving holiness or merely loving the experience. 5. If your understanding feels small, take heart, and ask. This light has never been distributed according to cleverness.

A PRAYER
Father, I have read Your Word for years and there are pages I have never seen. I know a great deal about You that has never once moved me.
I cannot manufacture sight. Flesh and blood will not reveal this. So I ask You, who commanded light to shine out of darkness, to shine in my heart.
Do not give me new revelations; give me eyes for what You have already written. Let me taste and see that You are good, and having tasted, let me want nothing else so much. Amen.

fields.title: The Excellency of Christ
fields.body_html:
Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda …and I beheld, and, lo, in the midst of the throne …stood a Lamb as it had been slain. REVELATION 5:5–6

One of Edwards’s most beautiful sermons takes its text from the scene in heaven where the sealed book is opened. John is told to behold a Lion. He turns, and sees a Lamb. Edwards seized on that. In one Person, in one moment, in one verse: the fiercest of creatures and the gentlest, the conqueror and the sacrifice. And he built from it the theme he called an admirable conjunction of diverse excellencies in Christ Jesus.

Qualities that do not normally combine

His argument depends on an observation about human beings that we all recognise from experience. In creatures, excellencies tend to exclude one another. A man of towering authority is rarely gentle; a gentle man is rarely commanding. Strict justice and abundant mercy pull against each other in every human judge who has ever tried to hold both. Great dignity does not sit easily with genuine lowliness. We admire people who manage a partial balance, and we notice how rare it is. In Christ, Edwards said, qualities that in anyone else would be incompatible are found together at their highest degree, and without the least strain. Infinite majesty, and the humility of a servant. He is Lord of glory, and He washed feet. Perfect justice, and boundless mercy. He does not relax the law in order to forgive; He satisfies it, and forgives. Absolute sovereignty, and complete submission. He upholds all things by the word of His power, and He said not my will, but thine, be done. Supreme worthiness of all honour, and patience under the worst dishonour ever offered.

Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: but made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant …and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. PHILIPPIANS 2:6–8

Edwards’s point is not that Christ alternates between these — majestic on Sunday, meek on Monday. It is that they meet in Him simultaneously, and that their meeting is what makes Him unspeakably attractive.

Where the conjunction is clearest

If you want to see it, he said, look at the cross. At Calvary, Christ’s obedience is at its highest and His suffering is at its deepest. His love for sinners and His hatred of sin appear in the same act. His divine glory is most hidden and most displayed at once. The Lion is never more a Lion than when He submits as a Lamb, because it is by dying that He conquers.

He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief …he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities. ISAIAH 53:3, 5

This is why Edwards regarded the gospel not merely as true but as beautiful. A salvation in which God simply overlooked sin would be less lovely, because justice would have been sacrificed. A salvation in which God merely punished would be less lovely, because mercy would have been absent. What actually happened is more glorious than either, and no one would have invented it.

What this does for the sinner

The pastoral use of the doctrine is direct, and Edwards pressed it hard. The conjunction of excellencies means there is no state a sinner can be in which does not find its answer in Christ. Are you afraid of Him? Look at the Lamb. Do you doubt He can help you? Look at the Lion. Do you fear your sin is too great for mercy? His mercy is infinite. Do you fear that mercy means God does not take your sin seriously? Look at what it cost Him.

Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart. MATTHEW 11:28–29

Edwards observed that the One with the most right to be unapproachable is the most approachable Person who has ever existed — and that this combination, once seen, does more to draw a sinner than any amount of argument.

There is a lesson here about how to commend Christ to others. We often try to make the gospel attractive by minimising its harder aspects — softening the holiness, muting the judgment. Edwards’s approach is the opposite, and far more powerful. Show both. Show the Lion and the Lamb. The beauty is in the conjunction, and a Christ trimmed to be inoffensive is not more attractive. He is merely smaller.

The Lamb remains a Lamb

There is a detail in the vision that Edwards did not let pass, and it has consequences. When John turns to see the Lion, what he sees is a Lamb as it had been slain — bearing, in glory, the marks of having been killed. This is not a memory of the cross. It is the risen and reigning Christ, and He still carries the wounds.

And they sung a new song, saying, Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood. REVELATION 5:9

The worship of heaven, in other words, is organised around the crucifixion. The song is not about power in the abstract; it is about a slain Lamb who purchased people at a price. Whatever else eternity contains, the centre of it is the death of Christ for sinners, contemplated for ever by those it saved. Edwards drew two things from this. The first is that the condescension of Christ is not a temporary phase now concluded. We might imagine the humility of the incarnation as a season He passed through and left behind on returning to glory. The vision says otherwise. The Lamb is on the throne. The lowliness has been taken up into the glory permanently, which is why the conjunction of excellencies is not an episode but His abiding character. The second is pastoral, and it goes to the heart of Christian assurance. The One who will judge the world is the One who was judged in the sinner’s place, and He appears in the judgment scene still bearing the evidence.

For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. HEBREWS 4:15

Edwards pressed the encouragement hard. A believer approaching God is not approaching a stranger to his condition. He comes to One who has been hungry, exhausted, betrayed, misunderstood by His family, abandoned by His friends and executed by the state — and who has not put any of that down.

Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need. HEBREWS 4:16

Boldly, to a throne. The two words do not naturally belong together anywhere else in the universe.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read Revelation 5 slowly and stop at the moment John turns. Ask what it means that the Lion is a Lamb. 2. Take the pair of qualities in Christ you find hardest to hold together — perhaps His severity and His tenderness — and meditate on the cross, where both appear at once. 3. Notice whether you have quietly trimmed Christ to make Him easier to commend. Restore what you removed. 4. Bring to Him the specific fear that makes you hesitant to approach, and answer it from His character rather than from your performance. 5. Tell someone this week something about Christ that you find beautiful, not merely something you believe is true.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You are the Lion and the Lamb, and I have rarely held both in view at once.
I have made You gentle and forgotten Your majesty, or made You awful and forgotten Your meekness. Forgive me for the smaller Christ I have carried in my mind.
Show me the excellencies that meet in You — justice and mercy, glory and lowliness, sovereignty and obedience — and let the sight of them draw me as no argument ever could.
You are worthy. Let me behold You, and be changed. Amen.

It is the risen and reigning Christ, and He still carries the wounds. And they sung a new song, saying, Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood. The second is pastoral, and it goes to the heart of Christian assurance. The One who will judge the world is the One who was judged in the sinner’s place, and He appears in the judgment scene still bearing the evidence. For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. HEBREWS 4:15 Edwards pressed the encouragement hard. A believer approaching God is not approaching a stranger to his condition. He comes to One who has been hungry, exhausted, betrayed, misunderstood by His family, abandoned by His friends and executed by the state — and who has not put any of that down. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need. HEBREWS 4:16 Boldly, to a throne. The two words do not naturally belong together anywhere else in the universe. FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Read Revelation 5 slowly and stop at the moment John turns. Ask what it means that the Lion is a Lamb. 2. Take the pair of qualities in Christ you find hardest to hold together — perhaps His severity and His tenderness — and meditate on the cross, where both appear at once. 3. Notice whether you have quietly trimmed Christ to make Him easier to commend. Restore what you removed. 4. Bring to Him the specific fear that makes you hesitant to approach, and answer it from His character rather than from your performance. 5. Tell someone this week something about Christ that you find beautiful, not merely something you believe is true. Forgive me for the smaller Christ I have carried in my mind. Show me the excellencies that meet in You — justice and mercy, glory and lowliness, sovereignty and obedience — and let the sight of them draw me as no argument ever could. You are worthy. Let me behold You, and be changed. Amen.

fields.title: The Beauty of Holiness
fields.body_html:
O worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness: fear before him, all the earth. PSALM 96:9

Ask most Christians what holiness is, and you will get an answer about rules. Holiness is not doing certain things; it is separation, restraint, moral seriousness. All of which is true, and all of which Edwards would have said misses the centre entirely. For Edwards, holiness is first of all beautiful. It is the moral loveliness of God, and the reason we so often experience it as a burden is that something has gone wrong with our capacity to perceive beauty.

Holiness as loveliness

In the Personal Narrative, describing the change that came over him after his conversion, he wrote about how holiness itself began to appear to him. It struck him as sweet, pleasant, charming, serene and calm — language no one would use of a rulebook. He described the soul in a state of holiness under the figure of a flower in a field, opening to the sun, quietly receiving light, giving off fragrance, harming nothing. That is a long way from the grim caricature attached to his name, and it is the authentic Edwards. Holiness is not the absence of pleasure; it is the presence of a superior order of pleasure. It is what a human being looks like when everything in him is rightly proportioned and rightly aimed.

One thing have I desired of the Lord, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the Lord, and to enquire in his temple. PSALM 27:4

Sin as deformity

If holiness is beauty, then sin is not merely rule-breaking. It is ugliness — disorder, distortion, a thing out of proportion. Edwards found this a far more penetrating way of exposing sin than the merely legal one, and it is worth seeing why. A man can hear that a certain action is forbidden and feel only that a restriction has been placed on him. He may comply resentfully, looking for the boundary of the rule. But if he is shown that the thing is ugly — that his envy is a deformity, that his self-importance is grotesque, that his harshness with his family is a species of squalor — something different happens. He does not want it any more.

Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice; and be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you. EPHESIANS 4:31–32

Put those two verses side by side and consider which is the more beautiful human being. That question, Edwards thought, is not sentimental. It is theological, and it goes deeper than duty.

Why this changes obedience

The consequence for the Christian life is considerable. If holiness is a rule, obedience is compliance, and compliance is always grudging at the margins. We keep what we must and negotiate the rest. Our sanctification becomes a matter of managing behaviour, and we measure progress by how little we have broken. If holiness is beauty, obedience becomes desire. We pursue it as a man pursues anything he finds lovely — not because he is required to, but because he wants it. This is why Edwards insisted that the will is never moved by bare duty alone. The heart follows what it finds attractive. The whole work of grace, in his view, is to change what a person finds attractive, and everything else follows from that.

Delight thyself also in the Lord; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart. PSALM 37:4

There is a practical implication for how we teach, and especially for how we raise children in the faith. A generation instructed only in prohibitions will keep them while supervised and abandon them at the first opportunity, because nothing has been done to their affections. A generation shown that God is beautiful, that holiness is lovely and sin is squalid, has been given something that survives the removal of supervision. Edwards’s own preaching bears this out. He described sin’s ugliness relentlessly — but he spent far more time on the loveliness of Christ, because he believed that only a rival beauty can dislodge an old affection.

Shadows of divine things

Edwards kept a private notebook throughout his life which he headed Images of Divine Things. In it he recorded the ways the natural world seemed to him to picture spiritual realities. The rising sun and the coming of grace. The way a river finds the sea.

The silkworm that spins its covering and dies in the labour. The fact that the most beautiful flowers grow in soil made of decay. Hundreds of such entries, made over decades by a man walking and riding through the Connecticut Valley with his mind never off the subject. This was not idle fancy. It followed directly from his theology of glory. If God made the world to communicate His own fullness, then the world is a kind of language, and everything in it means something beyond itself.

The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork. PSALM 19:1
For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made. ROMANS 1:20

The practical value of this habit is considerable, and it is available to anybody. Most of us pass through a day registering almost nothing. We see weather rather than glory, and traffic rather than providence. Edwards trained himself to look at ordinary things until they yielded something, and the discipline seems to have been a substantial part of how his affections stayed warm through decades of routine. There is a caution to attach. Edwards’s readings are sometimes strained, and a reader can slide into finding secret meanings everywhere, which is a different activity and a less healthy one. The natural world illustrates truth; it does not supply new doctrine. Scripture governs. But held soberly, the habit is a gift. The believer who has learned to see a sunrise as more than a sunrise — who notices that seed dies before it grows, that light travels vast distances to arrive silently, that a river cannot be prevented from reaching the sea — has been given a thousand daily occasions for worship where he previously had none.

O Lord, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all: the earth is full of thy riches. PSALM 104:24
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Take one sin you tolerate. Stop asking whether it is permitted and ask whether it is beautiful. Sit with the answer. 2. Read Psalm 27:4 and ask whether beholding God’s beauty is genuinely among the things you desire, or only among the things you approve of.

3. Name a believer whose holiness you find attractive rather than merely impressive. Ask what makes the difference, and pursue that. 4. If you teach or raise children, audit what you say. What proportion is prohibition, and what proportion is the loveliness of Christ? 5. Ask God this week not merely for the strength to obey but for the desire to — for a changed taste rather than a stronger grip.

A PRAYER
Father, You are beautiful, and I have treated Your holiness as a burden to be carried rather than a glory to be enjoyed.
Show me the ugliness of the sin I have been excusing — not only its guilt, but its squalor. And show me the loveliness of Christ, until the comparison does what argument never has.
I do not merely want the strength to obey You. I want to want You. Change my taste, and let obedience follow desire, as it does in every heart that has seen what You are like. Amen.

fields.title: Original Sin
fields.body_html:
Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me. PSALM 51:5

The last book Edwards saw through the press, published in the year he died, was a defence of the doctrine that human nature is corrupt from birth. He wrote it against a popular treatise by an English minister who held that men are born morally neutral and become sinners only by imitation and bad example. The disagreement sounds technical. It is in fact the difference between two entirely different religions, because everything depends on what is wrong with us.

The argument from the evidence

Edwards’s opening move was not a proof text. It was an appeal to the record. If human beings are born neutral, and sin is merely learned, then somewhere in the history of the world we should expect to find a person who did not learn it, or a society that avoided it. There is no such person and no such society. The pattern is universal, it appears in every culture that has ever existed, and it appears early — long before a child has had time to be corrupted by example. Universal effects, he argued, require a universal cause. A tree that produces bad fruit in every soil and climate has something wrong with the tree.

And God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually. GENESIS 6:5
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? JEREMIAH 17:9

Note the second half of that verse, which Edwards found particularly important. Not only is the heart corrupt; it is corrupt in a way that hides itself from the person whose heart it is. Sin includes its own concealment. This is why self-examination is unreliable and why we are most confident precisely where we are most blind.

Not acts but disposition

The heart of the doctrine is that sin is a condition before it is a behaviour.

Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned. ROMANS 5:12

We are not sinners because we sin; we sin because we are sinners. The acts are symptoms. And this explains something every honest person notices about himself: that his failures are not random accidents but have a consistent direction. The same faults recur across decades. Something is bent, not merely occasionally misused. Edwards described the essence of that bentness with unusual precision. Man was made to love God supremely and all other things in proportion to their worth. In the fall, that ordering collapsed, and the self moved into the position God had occupied. What remains is not the absence of love but love wrongly centred — a private system in which everything is valued by its usefulness to me. This accounts for why so much apparent virtue is hollow. A man may be generous, disciplined and kind, and be so entirely for himself — for his reputation, his self-image, his comfort. The behaviour is admirable and the centre is unchanged.

Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh …and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others. EPHESIANS 2:3

By nature. Not by choice, not by imitation. By what we are.

Where Edwards is contested

Honesty requires a note here, and it concerns not the doctrine but Edwards’s particular explanation of it. The difficulty every theologian faces is how we can be justly implicated in the act of a man who lived before us. Edwards’s answer, worked out in the later part of the treatise, is that the unity of the human race with Adam rests on a divine constitution — that identity over time, even the identity of a single person with himself from one moment to the next, is not a natural fact but something God continuously establishes. On that basis, God constitutes the race one with its head. It is an ingenious argument and it has never commanded general assent. Many careful readers who hold the doctrine of original sin firmly find this particular account speculative, and some think it proves too much. Others prefer the more traditional explanation of Adam as covenant head representing his posterity.

The reader should feel free to hold the doctrine and set the explanation aside. Scripture asserts the fact plainly and does not supply the mechanism. Edwards’s attempt to supply one is interesting; it is not binding.

The practical value of this doctrine is that it makes the gospel intelligible. If the problem were bad habits, we would need instruction. If it were bad company, we would need a better environment. If it were ignorance, we would need education. Christianity has been repeatedly reduced to each of these, and each reduction produces a religion of self-improvement. If the problem is a corrupt nature, then nothing will do but a new birth — and that is precisely what is offered.

Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again. JOHN 3:7

The kindness of a severe diagnosis

It is worth pausing to notice that this doctrine, which sounds so bleak, is in several respects a mercy. A severe diagnosis is kinder than a false one. If a man is gravely ill, the physician who tells him he is a little run down and should take more exercise is not being gentle; he is killing him politely. The doctor who names the disease accurately is the one who can treat it. Edwards understood the alternative accounts on offer, and they have only multiplied since. We are told our problems are the result of upbringing, environment, poor education, unmet needs, or bad social arrangements. Each contains truth. None accounts for the universality of the pattern, and each locates the fault somewhere other than in the person himself — which sounds compassionate and leaves him helpless, since he cannot change his history. There is also an equality in this doctrine that is easily missed and worth dwelling on. If sin is a condition we all share from birth, then the ground before God is entirely level. The respectable and the disgraced differ in how far the disease has visibly progressed, not in whether they have it. The person whose sins are socially acceptable — coldness, pride, quiet contempt, comfortable indifference to suffering — is not further along than the person whose sins are visible and shameful. He is merely better camouflaged.

For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God. ROMANS 3:23

This is why Edwards regarded the doctrine as an enemy of self-righteousness rather than a source of despair. Nobody who genuinely believes it can look down on anyone, because he has no ground on which to stand and look down from. And it makes the gospel proportionate. A God who offered advice to people who needed only advice would be adequate. A God who raises the dead is what the situation actually requires.

Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ; (by grace ye are saved). EPHESIANS 2:5

Dead people are not improved. They are raised, or they stay as they are. That is the whole difference between Christianity and every scheme of moral betterment that has ever been proposed.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Look at your recurring faults over ten years, not ten days. Ask what the consistency of their direction tells you. 2. Take one genuinely good thing you have done recently and examine the centre of it. Who was it finally for? 3. Stop treating your sin as a series of incidents to be managed and start treating it as a condition to be healed. 4. Where you feel most confident of your own integrity, ask God to search you there specifically. That is where Jeremiah 17:9 applies. 5. Thank God for the new birth — a remedy proportionate to the actual disease.

A PRAYER
Lord, I have wanted to believe my sins are incidents, and You tell me they are symptoms.
I confess that the fault is not in my circumstances or my upbringing or the people around me. It is in me, and it was in me before I could choose it.
Search me where I am most sure of myself, for that is where I am most deceived.
And thank You that You did not offer me instruction when I needed resurrection. I cannot reform what You have said must be born again. Do in me what only You can do. Amen.

fields.body_html:
And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life. JOHN 5:40

In 1754, from a frontier village, Edwards published the book that made his reputation as a philosopher. Its full title is forbidding and its argument is dense, but the distinction at its centre is one of the most practically useful tools in pastoral theology. It answers a question every believer eventually asks. If a sinner cannot come to God without grace, how can he be blamed for not coming?

Two kinds of cannot

Edwards’s answer turns on distinguishing two things we confuse because English uses one word for both. There is natural inability. A man cannot fly. A prisoner in chains cannot leave. A blind man cannot see the sunrise. In each case something outside the person’s will prevents him, and nobody holds him responsible. We do not blame the prisoner for staying in his cell. There is moral inability. A devoted mother cannot bring herself to harm her child. A man of settled integrity cannot be induced to betray his friend. Here nothing external prevents anything. The person has every faculty required. What he lacks is the inclination — and the stronger his character, the more truly we say he cannot. Notice that in the second case, the inability is not an excuse. It is a description of the person’s heart, and we praise or blame people precisely for this kind of cannot. The sinner’s inability, Edwards argued, is entirely of the second kind. He has understanding, will and conscience. Nothing binds his hands. What he lacks is any desire for God — and that lack is not his misfortune, it is his sin.

No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him. JOHN 6:44
Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be. ROMANS 8:7

Both verses say cannot. Neither offers it as an excuse. Set them beside ye will not come to me, and the two are the same fact described from two angles: the cannot is a will not.

What freedom actually is

Behind this lies Edwards’s account of the will itself. He argued that the will is not some neutral faculty hovering above our desires, choosing between them from a position of indifference. The will always follows what appears most desirable to the person at the moment of choosing. We invariably choose what we most want. Freedom, then, is not the power to choose against your strongest desire — which would be a strange thing to want, and would make every choice random rather than responsible. Freedom is being able to act according to your desire without external constraint. The prisoner is unfree; the man who stays home because he prefers to is entirely free, even though his choice was certain. This is why responsibility survives. You are responsible not because your choices were uncaused, but because they were yours — they came from what you actually wanted.

Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil. JEREMIAH 13:23

Where readers differ

This is Edwards’s most philosophically contested work, and readers should know it. Many thoughtful Christians hold that genuine moral responsibility requires the real ability to have chosen otherwise, and that Edwards’s account, however carefully argued, ultimately makes God the author of sin. Others find the distinction between natural and moral inability decisive and the objection answered. The debate has continued for two and a half centuries without resolution, and it will not be settled here. What is not in dispute among those who take Scripture seriously is the pastoral substance: that sinners are genuinely unable to save themselves, that they are genuinely responsible, and that both are taught in the same passages.

The practical use of the distinction is considerable, and it works in two directions. It removes the sinner’s excuse. A person who says he would come to Christ if he could is invited to examine what is actually stopping him. Nothing external is. He does not come because he does not want to, and that is not a limitation to be pitied but a heart to be repented of. And it directs prayer accurately. If the obstacle were natural, we would need circumstances changed. Because it is moral, we ask God to change the wanting. That is precisely what He has promised to do.

A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. EZEKIEL 36:26

Both at once

The obvious question raised by this chapter is how divine sovereignty and human responsibility can both be fully true. Edwards’s answer, stripped of its philosophical machinery, is that Scripture asserts both without apology and we are not at liberty to drop either. The clearest case is the one every Christian already accepts without noticing.

Wherefore, my beloved …work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure. PHILIPPIANS 2:12–13

Notice the logic of that for. Paul does not say: work hard, because God has done His part and the rest is up to you. He says: work, because God is at work in you — and God’s work extends to the willing itself. The divine activity is offered as the ground of the human activity, not its replacement. This is the pattern throughout Scripture. God commands what only He can give, and gives what He commands.

Make you a new heart and a new spirit: for why will ye die, O house of Israel? EZEKIEL 18:31
A new heart also will I give you …and I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes. EZEKIEL 36:26–27

The same prophet, in the same book, commands the people to make themselves a new heart and promises that God will give them one. Edwards regarded this as decisive. If the two were genuinely incompatible, Ezekiel would not have written both. The practical consequence is a refusal of both errors that this doctrine tends to produce. The first error is fatalism — the conclusion that since God is sovereign, effort is pointless. Edwards’s response is that God ordains means as well as ends, and that our striving is one of the means through which He accomplishes His purpose. Nobody argues that since God has appointed the harvest we need not plant. The second error is self-reliance — treating the commands as though we could meet them unaided. That is precisely the error the whole treatise exists to demolish. The believer’s position is therefore to work as hard as if it depended on him, and to pray as one who knows perfectly well that it does not.

Edwards saw no tension there at all, and neither, apparently, did Paul.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Where you say you cannot obey God in some matter, test which kind of cannot it is. Is anything actually preventing you but your own unwillingness? 2. Change how you pray for the unconverted. Ask God to give them a new wanting, not merely a new opportunity. 3. Stop waiting to feel willing before you act. Obedience frequently precedes desire, and desire follows. 4. Hold this doctrine with humility. Sincere believers differ here, and it is not a test of orthodoxy. 5. Take Ezekiel 36:26 as a personal request for the area of your life that feels most immovable.

A PRAYER
Lord, I have said that I could not, when the truth is that I would not.
Take away the excuse. Show me that nothing stands between me and obedience except a heart that does not want what You want.
I cannot repair my own wanting. So I ask for what You promised: take out the heart of stone and give me a heart of flesh.
Make me willing, and then hold me to it. Amen.
