fields.title: Justification by Faith Alone
fields.body_html:
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. ROMANS 4:5

In November 1734 Edwards preached a series of sermons at Northampton on justification by faith alone. He was answering a drift in New England towards a comfortable moralism in which decent behaviour was quietly assumed to secure God’s favour. What followed was not a theological controversy. It was a revival. Within months the town was transformed, and Edwards always maintained that the doctrine and the awakening were connected — that people were converted precisely when they stopped trying to contribute.

Justifying the ungodly

The scandal is in the text, and Edwards would not let his hearers soften it. Paul does not say that God justifies the repentant, or the sincere, or those doing their best. He says God justifies the ungodly. The person declared righteous is, at the moment of the declaration, not righteous.

Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus …Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law. ROMANS 3:24, 28

Justification is a legal declaration, not a description of our condition. God does not inspect us and find us acceptable. He credits to us a righteousness that belongs to another and treats us accordingly.

And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith. PHILIPPIANS 3:9

How faith justifies — and how it does not

Here Edwards made a distinction of great precision, and it protects the doctrine from the most common way of ruining it. The natural assumption is that faith is the one thing God accepts in place of works — that whereas the law demanded obedience we could not render, the gospel demands only belief, which we can manage. On that view faith has become a very small work, and we are back to being saved by something we do. Edwards rejected this firmly. Faith does not justify as a virtue, as though God were rewarding us for believing. Faith justifies because it unites us to Christ. Its whole value is in its object. The illustration usually given is exact: a drowning man is not saved by the excellence of his grip but by the strength of the one who holds him. A weak hand on a strong rescuer is enough. A strong hand on nothing is not. This is why assurance need not depend on the quality of our believing. The question is not whether your faith is impressive but whether Christ is sufficient.

Justification and the life that follows

Edwards was equally firm at the other boundary, and this matters, because he is sometimes read as though his emphasis on holy living compromises free justification. It does not. He held both, and he held them in the biblical order. Justification is by faith alone, entirely apart from works, received at once and complete. And the faith that justifies is never alone — it invariably produces a changed life, because it unites us to a living Christ, and union with Him cannot leave a person as he was.

For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them. EPHESIANS 2:10

Works are the evidence, never the ground. Edwards’s later insistence on Christian practice as the great sign of grace, which we shall come to, rests entirely on this footing. He was not adding works to faith. He was pointing out that a tree is known by its fruit without the fruit having grown the tree.

There is a reason this doctrine produced revival rather than complacency, and it is worth understanding, because we might expect the opposite. Moralism is exhausting and it never delivers assurance, because the standard is always just beyond reach and the conscience is never quiet. What it produces is either despair or self-deception. Free justification ends the exhaustion. And the person who has actually stopped paying discovers that gratitude motivates far more powerfully than fear ever did. Edwards watched a whole town discover this in a single winter.

The great exchange

Behind the doctrine of justification lies a transaction that Scripture states with startling economy.

For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:21

Two transfers in a single sentence, running in opposite directions. Our sin is reckoned to Christ, who had none. His righteousness is reckoned to us, who have none. Neither transfer is a legal fiction in the sense of a pretence; both rest on a real union, which is why faith — the instrument of that union — is the means by which the whole thing is received. Edwards laid stress on the completeness of what is credited. The righteousness imputed is not a fresh start, a clean sheet, or a reduced sentence. It is the entire active and passive obedience of Christ — everything He did in His life and everything He bore in His death — placed to our account. This means the believer does not stand before God as forgiven but unproven. He stands as one who has kept the law perfectly, because Another kept it for him.

For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. ROMANS 5:19

The practical weight of this falls on assurance, and it addresses the most common disorder among sincere Christians. Believers who understand that their sins are forgiven often still live as though their standing fluctuates — better after a good week, worse after a bad one. The reason is that they are thinking only of the first transfer. Forgiveness removes a debt and leaves the account at zero, and from zero one must presumably begin earning again. The second transfer ends that arithmetic. The account is not at zero; it is full, and it was filled by someone whose performance does not vary. There is nothing to earn, because nothing is missing.

There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus. ROMANS 8:1

Edwards preached this to a congregation that had spent generations quietly assuming that respectability counted for something with God. Within months, a town that had been trying to be good enough discovered it had never needed to be, and could not stop talking about it.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask whether you are trusting Christ or trusting the quality of your trust. The difference determines where you look when assurance falters. 2. Identify one way you are still trying to earn God’s favour. Name it, and renounce it specifically. 3. Read Romans 4:5 aloud and let the phrase justifieth the ungodly stand without qualification. 4. Check the order in your own thinking: are good works your ground of acceptance, or the evidence of it? 5. When you fail this week, do not set about repairing your standing. Return to a righteousness that was never yours in the first place.

A PRAYER
Father, I have been trying to bring You something.
You justify the ungodly, and I have laboured for years to arrive at Your court as something other than that. Forgive the pride hidden in all my striving.
I have no righteousness of my own. I take the righteousness of Christ, credited to me, which I did not earn and cannot lose.
And now that nothing depends on my performance, let gratitude do in me what fear never could. Amen.

fields.title: Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God
fields.body_html:
Their foot shall slide in due time. DEUTERONOMY 32:35

On the eighth of July, 1741, Edwards rode to Enfield, a town that had so far been untouched by the awakening spreading through the valley, and preached the sermon everyone remembers. He did not shout it. By all accounts he read it in a level voice from a manuscript held close to his short-sighted eyes, with little gesture. The congregation began crying out before he had finished, and he had to pause. The power was not in the delivery.

What he actually argued

The doctrine drawn from the text is a single sentence: there is nothing keeping wicked men out of hell at any moment except the mere pleasure of God. Everything else in the sermon is an unfolding of that. The unconverted are not safe because they are healthy, because they are respectable, because they intend to repent later, or because nothing has happened to them yet. They are suspended over destruction by nothing but the will of the God they have offended. The images are famous and they are relentless. A bow bent, the arrow on the string. Waters dammed and rising. A spider held over a flame. Rotten ground underfoot that gives way without warning.

It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. HEBREWS 10:31

Modern readers find this intolerable, and it is worth asking honestly why. Part of the reason is that we have lost any strong sense that sin is an outrage against an infinitely worthy God. Edwards’s logic here follows directly from his first principle: if God’s worth is infinite, then contempt for Him is infinitely serious, and the punishment is not disproportionate at all.

The half nobody quotes

What is almost never quoted is where the sermon goes. Having spent the doctrine section establishing the danger, Edwards turns to the application, and the application is not condemnation. It is invitation. He tells his hearers that this is an extraordinary opportunity — a day when Christ has flung the door of mercy wide open and stands calling. He points to others already coming in. Three cautions are necessary, and Edwards’s own body of work supplies all of them. First, this sermon is not representative. It rests on the glory of God, and it is always aimed at mercy. It is borrowing his most quotable paragraph and discarding his argument. Third, and this must be said plainly: this material has done real harm when misapplied. Name one person for whom you have grown comfortable with their being unconverted. Repent of the comfort.

Lord God, I have made my peace with things You have not made Your peace with.
I have believed in Your love and quietly stopped believing in Your judgment, and my urgency has drained away accordingly.
Restore to me a right sense of what is at stake — not a fear that paralyses, but a seriousness that moves me towards the people around me.
And keep me from cruelty. Let me never use terror as a tool, or press upon a bruised soul what belongs to the hardened. Give me the wisdom to know the difference. Amen.

fields.title: True Religion Consists in Holy Affections
fields.body_html:
Whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. 1 PETER 1:8

In 1746, with the Great Awakening behind him and its wreckage plainly visible, Edwards published A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections. It is his masterpiece, and it was written by a man who had watched thousands profess conversion and had lived long enough to see how many of them lasted. Its opening thesis is deceptively simple: true religion consists, in great part, in holy affections.

What he meant by affections

Everything depends on getting this word right, and modern English makes it difficult. By affections Edwards did not mean emotions in our sense — moods, feelings, the weather of the inner life. He meant the vigorous inclinations of the soul: the settled loves and hatreds, longings and aversions, by which a person is actually moved. An affection is what you are inclined towards with your whole self. He distinguished these carefully from what he called the passions, which are more sudden, more bodily, and more likely to overwhelm. Passions come and go. Affections direct a life. The claim, then, is not that religion consists in having strong feelings during worship. It is that religion consists in the heart being genuinely inclined towards God — and that where this inclination is absent, whatever else is present is not saving faith.

And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might. DEUTERONOMY 6:5

Against two errors at once

Edwards was writing between two parties, and the treatise attacks both. On one side stood those who concluded from the excesses of the revival that emotion in religion is inherently suspect — that the safe course is doctrine soberly held and duty quietly performed. Edwards regarded this as a catastrophic misreading of Scripture. The Bible commands love, joy, hope, godly sorrow, zeal, hunger and thirst. A religion that never engages the affections is not more spiritual than one that does; it is dead.

Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord. ROMANS 12:11
So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth. REVELATION 3:16

On the other side stood those who took any strong religious feeling as evidence of grace — who counted tears, ecstasies and dramatic experiences as proof. Edwards regarded this as equally disastrous, and the bulk of the treatise is devoted to dismantling it. His position is that the presence of strong affections proves nothing by itself, and their absence proves a great deal. Feeling is necessary but not sufficient. That is a harder line to hold than either extreme, and it is why the book satisfied neither party.

Why the heart is the issue

Behind this lies Edwards’s whole anthropology. He did not believe that the will is moved by reason alone. Knowledge that leaves the heart cold changes nothing — we all know a great many true things we do not act on. What actually moves a person is what he loves. The affections are therefore not a decorative addition to the Christian life; they are its engine. This is why a merely intellectual conversion is not conversion. A man may revise his opinions about God without his loves being touched at all, and he will remain exactly the person he was, better informed. And it explains the direction of Edwards’s whole ministry. If the heart follows what it finds beautiful, then the preacher’s task is not principally to inform or to persuade but to display — to hold up Christ until the affections move.

There is a diagnostic question here that is worth carrying about. Not: do you believe the right things? Many do who are unchanged. Not: do you feel strongly in church? Many do who are unchanged. But: what do you love? What genuinely delights you, grieves you, occupies you when nothing requires it? Those answers, Edwards thought, are the truest map of a soul that exists.

How much of Scripture is affection

Edwards supported his thesis by an argument from sheer volume, and it is worth following, because it is difficult to answer. Consider how much of what Scripture commands is an affection rather than an action.

We are commanded to love God and neighbour, which the Lord Himself identified as the greatest commandments. We are commanded to fear God, to hope in Him, to rejoice in Him always, to hunger and thirst after righteousness, to delight in His law, to be zealous of good works, to be fervent in spirit, to have compassion on the afflicted, to hate evil, to mourn over sin, to be thankful in everything, to long for the appearing of Christ. Every one of those is a state of the heart. None can be produced by decision alone, and none can be faked for long.

My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God? PSALM 42:2

Now consider the saints themselves. The Psalms, which are the church’s prayerbook, are almost entirely affection — longing, grief, exultation, dread, gratitude, rage at injustice. David dances. Jeremiah weeps. Paul is willing to be accursed for his kinsmen. The Lord Jesus weeps at a grave, is moved with compassion, rejoices in spirit, is grieved at hardness of heart, and sweats in agony in a garden.

Jesus wept. JOHN 11:35

Edwards’s conclusion was that a religion which engages the intellect and the will while leaving the affections untouched bears no resemblance to the religion described in the Bible. Whatever such a thing is, it is not what Scripture is talking about. He added one further observation, and it disposes of a common objection. People sometimes plead temperament — that they are simply not emotional by nature, and that their faith is quieter than others’. Edwards allowed for real differences of constitution. But he noticed that the same people who report themselves incapable of strong feeling in religion are frequently capable of considerable passion about money, politics, reputation, sport or family. The affections are working. The question is what they are attached to.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask what you actually delight in, as distinct from what you approve of. The gap between those two lists is the honest measure of your heart. 2. If your faith has become entirely cerebral, admit it. Ask God to move your affections, not merely to inform your mind.

3. If your faith runs on experiences, admit that too, and start testing them by the marks in the next chapters. 4. Notice what grieves you this week. Are you troubled by the things that grieve God, or only by the things that inconvenience you? 5. Spend time deliberately beholding Christ rather than analysing yourself. The affections follow the gaze.

A PRAYER
Lord, I have held true things about You without loving You, and I have felt strongly in Your presence without being changed.
Deliver me from a religion of the head that never reaches the heart, and from a religion of the feelings that never reaches the life.
Give me holy affections — real love for what You love, real grief over what grieves You, real longing for Your presence when nothing compels me.
Show me Christ until my heart moves. Amen.

fields.title: Distinguishing Marks
fields.body_html:
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God. 1 JOHN 4:1

In September 1741, at the height of the awakening, Edwards preached at the Yale commencement to an audience that included many of the movement’s fiercest critics. The address was published as The Distinguishing Marks of a Work of the Spirit of God. The situation demanded it. The revival had produced genuine conversions and also outcry, fainting, visions, itinerant preachers denouncing settled ministers, and men claiming direct messages from God. One party declared the whole thing a work of the Spirit; the other declared it hysteria. Edwards refused both, and set about supplying tests.

Nine things that prove nothing

The first half of the argument is negative, and it is the more original half. Edwards lists things which, contrary to what both parties assumed, are no evidence either way. That a work is unusual, or conducted in ways not seen before, proves nothing. God is not obliged to repeat His methods, and novelty is neither a recommendation nor an objection. That it produces bodily effects — tears, trembling, groaning, fainting, collapse — proves nothing. Edwards granted that a real apprehension of eternal things might well overwhelm a frame of flesh and blood. He also granted that such effects can be produced by suggestion, crowd excitement and imagination. Therefore they settle nothing. That there is a great deal of noise and talk about religion proves nothing. That people are strongly impressed in their imaginations proves nothing. That the preaching dwells much on terror proves nothing. That some who are affected are self-deceived proves nothing about the rest. And — this is the point his critics could not accept — that the movement contains errors, imprudences and even scandals proves nothing about its origin. Edwards observed that no revival in Scripture or history has ever been free of human folly, because revivals happen among human beings. The corruption of converts is not evidence against their conversion; it is evidence that they have not yet been perfected.

Five things that prove a great deal

Having cleared the ground, he takes his positive tests directly from 1 John 4, and they are as useful today as they were in 1741. Does it raise the esteem of Jesus? Where a work leads people to a higher view of Christ as the Son of God and the only Saviour, that is a mark Satan will not counterfeit, because it is against his interest.

Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God. 1 JOHN 4:2

Does it work against sin and worldliness? A movement that draws people away from worldly lusts and the pursuits of this life is not being driven by the god of this world, who has no interest in emptying his own kingdom. Does it increase regard for Scripture? Genuine work of the Spirit establishes people in the Word. Anything that leads people to prize their own impressions above the written Word — however spiritual it sounds — is moving the wrong way. Does it lead to truth? The Spirit of truth convinces people of things that are actually so: their own sinfulness, the reality of judgment, the sufficiency of Christ. Does it produce love to God and man? This is the mark Edwards weighted most heavily. Not excitement, not zeal, not activity — love. And he noted the counterfeit precisely: a fierce, censorious, divisive spirit that condemns other Christians while claiming superior spirituality is not the Spirit of God, whatever else it may be.

Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God. 1 JOHN 4:7

The lasting value of this little book is its refusal of the easy verdict. Both parties in 1741 wanted a single judgment: it is all God, or it is all delusion. Edwards insisted on the harder and more accurate position — that in any real move of God among real people, genuine grace and human excess will be mixed, and the work of discernment is to separate them rather than to endorse or condemn the whole. That remains the mature Christian posture, and it is uncomfortable in exactly the same way today.

Judging works, not hearts

Edwards attached an important limitation to everything in this chapter, and ignoring it has done a great deal of harm. The marks are given for judging a work — a movement, a ministry, a general phenomenon — and for examining oneself. They are not given for pronouncing on the spiritual state of individuals.

He was emphatic about this because the awakening had produced exactly that abuse. Confident young converts were declaring particular ministers unconverted, dividing congregations on the strength of their own discernment, and treating their impressions about other people’s souls as revelation. Edwards regarded this as one of the most damaging things that happened in those years, and he said so at real cost to his standing with the movement’s enthusiasts.

Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts. 1 CORINTHIANS 4:5

His reasoning was consistent with everything else he taught. If the heart is deceitful above all things and unknowable even to its owner, then our confidence about someone else’s inner state is absurd. We see conduct; we do not see the soul. God alone reads hearts, and He has not delegated the function.

For the Lord seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart. 1 SAMUEL 16:7

This does not mean we are forbidden all judgment. Edwards was clear that we may and must assess teaching, evaluate conduct, and exercise discipline in the church where sin is open. What is forbidden is the confident verdict on another’s standing before God. There is a rule of thumb implicit in his practice that is worth adopting. Apply the strictest tests to yourself and the most charitable reading to others. Most of us do the reverse instinctively, and call it discernment.

Charity suffereth long, and is kind …beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things. 1 CORINTHIANS 13:4, 7

Believeth all things, hopeth all things. That is not naivety. It is the posture of someone who knows he cannot see what only God can see, and who has decided which way to lean in the absence of certainty.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Apply the five positive tests to any movement or ministry you are assessing — including your own church, and including yourself. 2. Stop treating manifestations as evidence in either direction. Ask what they produce over five years, not what they look like in the moment.

3. Where you have dismissed a whole work because of its excesses, reconsider. Separate the wheat from the chaff instead of burning the field. 4. Watch for the counterfeit of the fifth mark: zeal that condemns other believers is not love, however spiritual it sounds. 5. Ask whether your own spiritual experiences have left you esteeming Christ more highly and loving people more truly. If not, hold them loosely.

A PRAYER
Lord, give me discernment without cynicism, and openness without gullibility. I am prone to one or the other and rarely to both at once.

One party declared the whole thing a work of the Spirit; the other declared it hysteria. Edwards refused both, and set about supplying tests. Apply the strictest tests to yourself and the most charitable reading to others. Most of us do the reverse instinctively, and call it discernment. Charity suffereth long, and is kind …beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things. 1 CORINTHIANS 13:4, 7 Believeth all things, hopeth all things. That is not naivety. It is the posture of someone who knows he cannot see what only God can see, and who has decided which way to lean in the absence of certainty. FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Ask what they produce over five years, not what they look like in the moment. 3. Where you have dismissed a whole work because of its excesses, reconsider. Separate the wheat from the chaff instead of burning the field. 4. Watch for the counterfeit of the fifth mark: zeal that condemns other believers is not love, however spiritual it sounds. 5. fields.title: Signs of Gracious Affections
fields.body_html:
Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. 2 CORINTHIANS 13:5

Having shown that strong religious feeling proves nothing by itself, Edwards faced the obvious question. What, then, does prove something? The longest part of Religious Affections answers it with twelve signs. They are not a checklist to be scored, and Edwards said so explicitly — he warned that no set of marks can enable us to judge another person’s heart with certainty, and that some of them are visible only to the person himself. They are given for self-examination, and they are pointed. Five of them are particularly searching.

Loved for Himself, or for His usefulness

The second sign asks what the affections are actually fixed upon. Counterfeit religious joy, Edwards observed, characteristically begins with the self. A person becomes convinced that God loves him, that he is forgiven, that he is destined for heaven — and from this arises great gladness. Notice that every element of that joy is about his own good fortune. God appears in it only as the source of his benefit. Gracious affections begin at the other end. They are drawn first by what God is in Himself — His holiness, His truth, His beauty — and the personal benefit follows as a consequence rather than founding the whole structure. The test is uncomfortable and it is fair. Would God still be lovely to you if He gave you nothing further? Is your delight in Him, or in your standing with Him?

Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. PSALM 73:25

Evangelical humiliation

The sixth sign is a particular kind of lowliness, and Edwards distinguished it sharply from a counterfeit. There is a natural humiliation — a sense of one’s own smallness, failure or inadequacy — which any person may feel and which produces mostly despair or self-pity. It is essentially a wounded self, still very much at the centre.

Evangelical humiliation is different. It is the sense of one’s own utter insufficiency arising from a sight of God’s holiness, and its effect is not despair but relief. The soul stops defending itself and is glad to. Edwards regarded this as one of the most reliable marks, and he noted its inversion: the more genuine grace a person has, the smaller he appears to himself. Growth in holiness is accompanied by a growing sense of remaining sin, which is why mature saints so often describe themselves in terms younger believers find excessive.

I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes. JOB 42:5–6

The temper of Christ

The eighth sign is the character of Jesus reproduced — what Edwards called the lamblike, dovelike spirit. Here he confronted the most damaging phenomenon of the awakening. A great many people had become extremely zealous and extremely harsh: quick to denounce, confident about others’ spiritual state, contemptuous of ministers they judged unconverted. They regarded their severity as evidence of their earnestness. Edwards’s judgment was blunt. A censorious, bitter, quarrelsome spirit is not a sign of grace no matter how orthodox its opinions, because it is not the temper of the Lamb.

Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart. MATTHEW 11:29

Symmetry, and an appetite that grows

The tenth sign is proportion. Grace produces a balanced character rather than a lopsided one. The counterfeit is recognisable: enormous zeal in one department and nothing in another — fierce about doctrine and careless about money, scrupulous in worship and cruel at home, generous in public and unkind in private. Real grace touches everything, unevenly perhaps, but everywhere. The eleventh sign is the most encouraging in the list. False affections tend to satisfy — the person feels he has arrived, and his hunger diminishes. Gracious affections do the opposite: the more a soul receives, the more it wants. Spiritual appetite increases with feeding.

Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled. MATTHEW 5:6

A word of pastoral caution, which Edwards himself supplied. These signs can be used destructively. A tender believer already prone to introspection may work through such a list and conclude he has no grace at all, when in fact the very anxiety he feels is evidence of a heart that cares. Edwards was aware of this and warned against endless self-examination. The signs are for occasional honest review, not for daily audit. And the remedy when they trouble you is not more inspection but more looking away — to Christ, in whom the assurance is finally located.

A new nature, not a new mood

Two further signs from the list deserve attention, because together they set the frame for all the others. The first sign is that gracious affections arise from a spiritual and supernatural influence on the heart — something genuinely new, not a heightened version of what was already there. This distinction runs through everything Edwards wrote about conversion. A natural person may be moved by religion in entirely natural ways. He may be stirred by beautiful music, gripped by a powerful speaker, frightened by thoughts of death, comforted by a sense of belonging. None of these requires the Spirit of God, and all of them can produce tears and resolutions and a temporary change of life. What grace produces is different in kind. It is a new spiritual sense — the capacity treated in chapter four — and it perceives an excellence in divine things that natural faculties cannot detect at all.

Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. JOHN 3:3

The seventh sign follows from this: gracious affections are attended with a change of nature. Edwards insisted that grace does not merely add religious activities to an unchanged person. It alters the disposition itself, so that what a person fundamentally wants is different. The change may be gradual in its outworking and is often invisible at first, but it is a change in the person, not merely in his behaviour or his schedule.

Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:17

He added a qualification that has comforted many. The old nature is not eradicated, and the change is not complete in this life. A true convert still finds sin in himself, sometimes to his dismay, and the presence of that struggle is not evidence against conversion. What would be evidence against it is the absence of the struggle — the person in whom nothing has been disturbed at all.

The test, then, is not have you had a powerful experience? but has something in you been permanently altered? Not: were you moved on that occasion. But: do you want different things than you did, and has it lasted?

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask the second sign’s question directly: is your joy chiefly that God is glorious, or chiefly that you are safe? 2. Watch how you speak of other Christians who differ from you. Zeal that turns harsh has failed the eighth sign. 3. Look for lopsidedness. Where is your religion strong in public and absent in private? 4. Test your appetite. Has receiving from God made you hungrier or more satisfied with your present state? 5. Do not audit yourself daily. Review honestly, then turn your eyes to Christ, where assurance actually rests.

A PRAYER
Lord, search me, but do not leave me examining myself for ever.
Show me whether I love You for what You are or only for what You give. Show me whether my zeal has turned bitter. Show me the corner of my life where I have allowed grace no entry.
Give me the lowliness that comes from seeing You rather than the self-pity that comes from seeing myself.
And make me hungrier. Whatever You have given me, let it leave me wanting more of You. Amen.

fields.title: Christian Practice
fields.body_html:
Ye shall know them by their fruits. MATTHEW 7:16

The twelfth and last sign in Religious Affections occupies more space than several of the others together, and Edwards left no doubt about its standing. Christian practice — how a person actually lives — is the chief evidence of grace, both to observers and to the believer himself. This is the conclusion of his life’s work on the question, and it is the most practically important thing he ever wrote.

Above every experience

The claim is stronger than we might expect from the theologian of the affections, and that is precisely what makes it significant. Edwards had spent his career defending the necessity of inward experience against those who wanted religion reduced to conduct. And having done so, he concluded that when it comes to evidence, conduct outranks experience — including our own memory of our own experiences. His reasoning is straightforward. An experience is a single event, remembered by a mind we already know to be self-deceiving, uncheckable by anyone else, and frequently improved in the retelling. A life is a long series of choices under varied pressure, visible to others, and very difficult to counterfeit for decades.

He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him. 1 JOHN 2:4
If ye love me, keep my commandments. JOHN 14:15

This carries a hard implication which Edwards did not soften. A person whose sole ground of assurance is a conversion experience years ago, unsupported by any subsequent alteration in how he lives, has weaker evidence than he supposes. The experience may have been genuine. But it is not the evidence he thinks it is.

Three qualities of the practice that counts

Not all obedience is evidence, and Edwards specified what kind is.

It must be universal. The believer does not select which commands suit him. Partial obedience is the signature of self-will, since a man who keeps the rules he agrees with is following himself. Edwards noted that we are most revealed by the command we quietly exempt ourselves from. It must be constant — maintained under pressure, not merely when convenient. Trial is the test, because trial is where motives are exposed. A religion that survives only in good weather has not been tested at all. And it must be persevering, continuing to the end of life. Edwards gave great weight to endurance, and it is one of the reasons he wrote after the awakening rather than during it. Anyone can be fervent in a season when everyone around them is fervent. What a movement produces ten years later is the measure of it.

But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. MATTHEW 24:13

Not works-righteousness

It is essential to see why this is not a retreat from the doctrine of chapter nine. Edwards is not saying that practice justifies. He is saying that practice evidences. Justification is by faith alone, apart from works, received complete at the moment of believing. The question here is a different one entirely: how does anyone — including you — know whether that faith is present? The answer Scripture gives is fruit. Fruit does not grow the tree; it shows what the tree is.

Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone. JAMES 2:17
Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven. MATTHEW 7:21

Edwards was careful to add that Christian practice does not mean sinless practice, and the qualification matters for the tender conscience. What is in view is the direction and the general course of a life, not the absence of failure. The believer sins, and repents, and returns. The pattern is one of continuing return. What is inconsistent with grace is not falling but settling — the comfortable arrangement in which a person maintains a religious identity alongside a sin he has no intention of leaving. The question is not have you failed? It is which direction are you facing when you get up?

The evidence nobody sees

Edwards laid particular weight on a part of Christian practice that no congregation can observe: what a believer does when he is entirely alone. His reasoning is simple. Public religion has an audience, and an audience is a motive. A man may pray well in a meeting, give generously where giving is noticed, and speak warmly of Christ in company, for reasons that have nothing to do with Christ. Remove the observers, and the motive is exposed.

But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly. MATTHEW 6:6

The Lord’s instruction, Edwards noted, is not merely about avoiding hypocrisy. It is about establishing a region of a person’s life in which the only possible audience is God — and therefore the only possible motive is God. He applied the same test to a range of hidden things. What occupies the mind when it is not directed at a task. What a person does with an unexpected free hour. How he behaves towards those who can do nothing for him and cannot damage him. What he thinks about while pretending to listen. Whether he gives when no record is kept.

But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth. MATTHEW 6:3

There is a searching corollary. If a believer’s secret life is empty — no private prayer, no reading that nobody knows about, no giving that goes unrecorded — then his religion consists entirely of the parts that are seen. That is not proof of anything, since seasons of dryness are real and common. But it is a question worth asking, and asking honestly, because the answer is available to no one else. Edwards himself is a useful case. He rose very early, spent long hours in the study, prayed while riding alone through the woods, and pinned scraps of paper to his coat to record thoughts on those rides. Almost none of that was visible to his congregation, and there was nothing to be gained from it socially. It is the best evidence we have about the man, precisely because it had no audience. The question is not what your church sees. It is what happens in the hours nobody records.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask what your life would suggest about your faith to someone who could observe it for a year without hearing you speak. 2. Find the command you have quietly exempted yourself from. Everyone has one. Name it. 3. Test constancy: does your obedience hold under pressure, or only when it costs little? 4. If your assurance rests entirely on a past experience, do not discard it — but ask what has happened since. 5. Distinguish falling from settling. Identify anything you have stopped intending to leave, and stop making peace with it.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You said that we would be known by our fruit, and I would rather be known by my beliefs, or by an experience I once had.
Show me the command I have excused myself from. Show me where my obedience is selective, and where it holds only while it is easy.
I do not ask to be spared failure — I ask that I would always be found turning back. Keep me from settling anywhere You have told me not to stay.
Make my life the evidence, and not merely my words. Amen.

fields.body_html:
For if ye love them which love you, what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same? MATTHEW 5:46

Among the works Edwards wrote at Stockbridge and never saw published was a short, dense dissertation called The Nature of True Virtue. It asks what genuine goodness actually is, and its answer exposes a great deal of respectable morality as something other than virtue.

Benevolence to being in general

Edwards’s definition is that true virtue consists most essentially in benevolence to Being in general — a settled goodwill towards all that exists, proportioned to its worth, and therefore directed first and supremely to God, who is the greatest and best of all beings. That sounds abstract until you see what it excludes. Consider a man who loves his family devotedly, is loyal to his friends, serves his town, and would die for his country. We would call him a good man, and in an important sense he is. But Edwards asks a searching question: what is the boundary of his goodwill, and why is it drawn there? If it extends to his own circle and stops, then it may be nothing more than self-love enlarged. The family is his family; the country is his country. What appears as generosity may be attachment to an extension of himself. Edwards called these private systems — limited communities of affection which look like virtue from inside and function as selfishness from outside.

And if ye do good to them which do good to you, what thank have ye? for sinners also do even the same. LUKE 6:33

The Lord’s argument is exactly Edwards’s. Loving those who love you proves nothing, because it is available to anyone and requires no grace at all.

Why it must begin with God

The reason true virtue must be directed first to God is not arbitrary. If goodwill is to be proportioned to worth, and God is infinitely worthy, then a virtue that leaves God out has failed at the most important point. It has allocated love carefully among lesser beings while ignoring the greatest. A man may be scrupulously fair to his neighbours and profoundly unjust to his Maker.

Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart …this is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. MATTHEW 22:37–39

Note the order, and note that the second is like the first — flowing from it, sharing its nature. Love for God, rightly held, necessarily enlarges the circle of love for others, because it reorients the whole self away from its own centre.

If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen? 1 JOHN 4:20

The doctrine that convicted its author

There is a painful and instructive postscript to this chapter, and it would be dishonest to omit it. Edwards wrote this dissertation while owning human beings. His own principle — that virtue must extend beyond every private system, that goodwill limited to one’s own circle is self-love wearing a respectable face — is precisely the argument that condemns slaveholding. He did not apply it. He drew the boundary of his benevolence around a community that excluded the people working in his house, and did not notice. Within one generation his students did notice. Samuel Hopkins and Edwards’s own son became prominent opponents of slavery, and they argued their case directly from this doctrine, maintaining that they were simply following their teacher’s logic to its proper end. They were right. This is worth sitting with, because it demonstrates something Edwards himself taught more forcefully than anyone: that a man may hold a true principle, teach it brilliantly, and remain blind to its application in the one place where it would cost him. The heart is deceitful above all things, and it is most deceitful where we most benefit. None of which makes the principle false. It makes it dangerous — which is what true principles generally are.

So the question this chapter puts is simple and inescapable. Where is the boundary of your goodwill? Not what you profess, but where your actual care runs out — which people fall outside it, and what advantage you gain from the line being drawn where it is.

Common virtue is still a good

Edwards took care to prevent a misreading that his argument invites, and the qualification matters greatly for how Christians regard the world around them. To say that natural affection is not true virtue is not to say it is worthless. Edwards held that the natural loves — of parents for children, of friends for one another, of citizens for their community — together with natural conscience, the sense of justice, pity for suffering and shame at cruelty, are real goods. They are God’s gifts, given to fallen people, and they restrain the world from being as bad as it could be. Without them human society would be unliveable.

For when the Gentiles, which have not the law, do by nature the things contained in the law …shew the work of the law written in their hearts. ROMANS 2:14–15

So the Christian is not to sneer at the decency of unbelievers, nor to pretend that the kind atheist is secretly a monster, nor to treat every virtue outside the church as hypocrisy. That posture is both false and repellent, and it has done enormous damage to the credibility of the gospel. What Edwards insisted upon is a narrower and more precise point: these goods, real as they are, do not amount to the thing God requires, because they leave the centre unchanged. A man may be admirable in every direction except the one that matters most, and be, at the root, still living for himself. The distinction is between what is genuinely good and what is savingly good. Common virtue restrains; it does not reconcile.

For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast. EPHESIANS 2:8–9

There is a practical use in holding this properly. It should make Christians generous in their assessment of others and severe in the assessment of themselves — able to recognise and praise goodness wherever it appears, while refusing to rest their own hope on any quantity of it. And it removes a common evangelistic error. The task is not to persuade decent people that they are secretly wicked. It is to show them that a life organised around any centre but God, however admirable its conduct, has missed the point of being alive.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Map the boundary of your practical benevolence. Who is inside it? Who is outside, and why? 2. Ask what you gain from that boundary being where it is. That question does most of the work. 3. Identify one group you find it easy to disregard. Do something concrete for one of them this month. 4. Test whether your love for family, church or nation is virtue or enlarged self-interest. Would it survive if they ceased to be yours? 5. Ask God to show you the application of a truth you hold that you have never allowed to cost you anything.

A PRAYER
Father, You are the greatest of all beings, and true goodness begins with loving You above everything.
I have drawn a circle around the people who are mine, and I have called my loyalty to them virtue. Show me where my goodwill stops, and why it stops there.
I know that I am most blind where I most benefit. Teach me to suspect myself exactly at the point where a truth would cost me something.
Enlarge my heart. Let me love what You love, without the boundary I have quietly drawn. Amen.

fields.title: Heaven is a World of Love
fields.body_html:
Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease. 1 CORINTHIANS 13:8

In 1738 Edwards preached a series through 1 Corinthians 13, published long afterwards as Charity and Its Fruits. The final sermon is called Heaven is a World of Love, and anyone who believes Edwards was a gloomy man should be required to read it before saying so again. It is the most tender thing he wrote, and it is the natural conclusion of everything else in this book.

The fountain and the stream

His governing image is a river. God, he said, is the fountain of love, as the sun is the fountain of light. In heaven that love is not rationed or interrupted; it pours out from God, fills every inhabitant, and flows back to Him in adoration and outward to one another in delight. The whole society is one circulation of love, and nothing obstructs it anywhere.

God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him. 1 JOHN 4:16

Edwards observed that on earth love is real but always impeded. We love, and we are misunderstood. We love, and we are jealous. We love, and the person dies. We love, and our own coldness returns. Every affection here is mixed with something that spoils it. In heaven every obstruction is gone. Love has perfect objects, perfect capacity to receive, perfect freedom of expression, perfect security, and endless duration. Nothing is withheld and nothing is lost.

And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away. REVELATION 21:4

Differences without envy

Edwards addressed a question that troubles many people, and his answer is one of the loveliest passages in his work. Scripture indicates that there will be differences in heaven — degrees of glory, varying capacities, some given more than others. Does that not introduce comparison, and with it the possibility of envy?

His answer is that envy is impossible there, because envy requires a self at the centre. Where love is perfect, each person’s joy in another’s greater glory is itself a source of happiness. The one with the smaller vessel is not diminished by the larger; he delights in it. And the one with the greater capacity does not look down but pours out. Every vessel is full. That is the point. A smaller cup filled to the brim is not less full than a larger one, and in a society without self-regard, the size of one’s neighbour’s cup is a matter of pure gladness.

What this does for now

Edwards did not treat heaven as a consolation to be produced at funerals. He treated it as a description of the direction in which the Christian life is already moving. If heaven is a world of love, then love is not an optional refinement of Christian character; it is the substance of the thing we are being prepared for. A person being fitted for that world is being made loving now, and a person growing harder is moving the wrong way whatever else is true of him. This is why the sermon sits where it does, at the end of a series on 1 Corinthians 13. Paul’s argument is that gifts pass away and love remains — which means that love is the only part of our present Christian experience that carries over unchanged.

And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity. 1 CORINTHIANS 13:13

Faith will become sight. Hope will become possession. Love simply continues, and grows.

There is a striking implication for how we think about our own deaths, and Edwards drew it out. For the believer, dying is not principally leaving. It is arriving in the society for which he has been in training, among people he will love perfectly and be loved by perfectly, in the presence of the Fountain.

Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory. JOHN 17:24

That is the last prayer of Christ for His people, and it is the whole of heaven in a sentence.

Heaven begun below

Edwards did not regard heaven as merely future. He held that the same love which fills that world is already at work in this one, in the church, in smaller measure and under difficulty — and that Christian fellowship is the outpost of the world to come.

No man hath seen God at any time. If we love one another, God dwelleth in us, and his love is perfected in us. 1 JOHN 4:12

That is a remarkable claim, and Edwards took it at full weight. The invisible God becomes visible in the mutual love of His people. A congregation in which believers genuinely love one another is not merely a pleasant social arrangement; it is a demonstration of God to a world that cannot see Him directly.

By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another. JOHN 13:35

This gives the ordinary business of church life a dignity it is rarely accorded. Bearing with a difficult brother, forgiving an old injury, refusing to repeat a piece of gossip, welcoming someone who brings nothing useful — these are not minor housekeeping matters. They are rehearsals, and they are evidence. Edwards drew a sober conclusion from this, and it should be stated plainly. A person who has no appetite for the company of God’s people, who finds their society tedious and their concerns trivial, has reason to examine what he imagines heaven will be. Heaven is not a private arrangement between the individual and God. It is a society, and its whole life is love.

We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren. 1 JOHN 3:14

He was equally clear about the direction of the traffic. Our love for one another is not something we generate in order to qualify; it is the overflow of a love received.

We love him, because he first loved us. 1 JOHN 4:19

Which means the remedy for a cold heart towards other Christians is not chiefly to try harder with them. It is to go back to the fountain. A person who has been freshly warmed by the love of God will generally find his patience with his brethren has improved without his having worked directly on it at all.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Test whether your idea of heaven is chiefly relief from trouble or union with God. The difference reveals what you actually want.

2. Where you are envious of another believer’s gifting, treat it as practice for a world where such envy will be impossible. Begin rejoicing now. 3. Ask whether you are becoming a more loving person year by year. If not, you are not being prepared for the place you say you are going. 4. Name one relationship where love is currently obstructed by something you control. Remove the obstruction. 5. Read 1 Corinthians 13 as a description of heaven rather than a wedding reading, and notice how it changes.

A PRAYER
Father, You are the fountain of love, and every love I have known here has been a stream running through broken ground.
Thank You that there is a world where nothing obstructs it — no jealousy, no misunderstanding, no coldness, no parting.
Prepare me for it. Make me a person who could be happy there: glad at another’s greater glory, free of the self that spoils everything.
And when my turn comes to go, let it not feel like leaving, but like arriving. Amen.

fields.title: The Resolutions
fields.body_html:
See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. EPHESIANS 5:15–16

Between 1722 and 1723, in his late teens and early twenties, Edwards drew up seventy resolutions governing how he intended to live. He kept them beside him and read them over once a week for years. They are among the most quoted and most misunderstood documents in his corpus.

The preface everyone skips

Before the first resolution, Edwards wrote a short preamble which changes the meaning of everything that follows, and which is almost always omitted when the list is reproduced. He states that he is unable to do anything without God’s help, and asks God by His grace to enable him to keep these resolutions, so far as they are agreeable to God’s will. Read the list without that, and it is a young man’s programme of self-improvement by willpower — and an oppressive one. Read it with the preamble, and it is something else entirely: a set of intentions laid before God by someone who has already conceded he cannot execute them. The distinction is exactly the one Edwards would spend his life defending. The resolutions do not produce grace. They are how a man who has received grace proposes to spend his time.

What he resolved

The themes recur, and they are worth listing because they show what a God-centred life looked like to him in practice. Time. He resolved never to lose one moment of time but to use it in the most profitable way he could. The urgency about time never left him, and it is connected to his view of eternity: a short life, an endless consequence.

So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. PSALM 90:12

Intensity. He resolved to live with all his might while he lived. Not to drift, not to coast, not to spend a life half-engaged.

The perspective of death. Several resolutions turn on a single device: to act now as he would wish he had acted when he came to die. He resolved never to do anything he would be afraid to do in the last hour of his life. It is a remarkably clarifying test, and it can be applied immediately by anyone.

Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city …Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour. JAMES 4:13–14

Scripture. He resolved to study the Scriptures steadily, constantly and frequently, so as to grow plainly in knowledge of them. The ordinary. A striking number concern eating, drinking, sleep, speech and temper — the unglamorous machinery of a life. The Diary he kept alongside these records a good deal of discouragement. He falls short repeatedly. He is dissatisfied with himself. There are stretches of spiritual dullness that he notes with distress. This should be said plainly, because the Resolutions have done harm to scrupulous readers. It is worth setting out how Edwards actually spent his days, because the Resolutions can give the impression of a man sustained by heroic acts of will, and the reality was far more ordinary and far more imitable.

fields.title: A Humble Attempt
fields.body_html:
Yea, many people and strong nations shall come to seek the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem, and to pray before the Lord. ZECHARIAH 8:22

The last of Edwards’s teachings to consider is the one with the longest reach, and it began as a proposal from Scotland. In 1744 a group of Scottish ministers agreed to set aside regular times to pray together for the revival of religion and the spread of the gospel, and invited others to join. Edwards took up the idea and in 1747 published a book to promote it, with a title as long as its argument was simple: An Humble Attempt to Promote Explicit Agreement and Visible Union of God’s People in Extraordinary Prayer for the Revival of Religion and the Advancement of Christ’s Kingdom on Earth.

The concert of prayer

The proposal itself was modest. Christians in different places and different denominations would agree to pray at the same appointed times — a quarterly day, and part of each week — for the same object: that God would pour out His Spirit and advance the gospel through the whole earth. Edwards’s argument for it rested on three things. Scripture promises a great advance. He took texts like Zechariah 8 and Isaiah’s visions of the nations streaming in as descriptions of something God actually intends to do in history, not merely poetry.

For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea. HABAKKUK 2:14

Scripture commands us to ask for it, persistently and without discouragement. He leaned on the parable of the importunate widow, and on Isaiah’s watchmen who are told to give God no rest until He establishes His purpose.

Ye that make mention of the Lord, keep not silence, and give him no rest, till he establish, and till he make Jerusalem a praise in the earth. ISAIAH 62:6–7

And union in prayer has a particular promise attached to it.

If two of you shall agree on earth as touching any thing that they shall ask, it shall be done for them of my Father which is in heaven. MATTHEW 18:19

Where the timetable was wrong

Honesty requires a note, because Edwards attached to this book a good deal of speculation about prophetic chronology — attempts to locate the present moment in the scheme of Revelation and to estimate how near the promised outpouring might be. He was mistaken, as everyone who has attempted such calculations has been mistaken, and the sections of the book devoted to them are the least valuable. It is worth noting that his own Master declined to supply this information (Acts 1:7), and that no one since has improved on that silence. Take the burden and leave the arithmetic. The command to pray persistently for the advance of the gospel does not depend on knowing when the answer arrives.

What it produced

The postscript to this book is remarkable, and Edwards did not live to see any of it. An Humble Attempt was read a generation later by a group of Baptist ministers in Northamptonshire, who in 1784 issued a call to united monthly prayer for the conversion of the nations. Among those who took it up was a young cobbler named William Carey. Carey went to India in 1793, and the modern Protestant missionary movement is usually dated from there. A book about prayer, written by a dismissed pastor on a frontier settlement, helped set in motion the largest missionary expansion in Christian history — after its author was dead.

This is the right place to end, because it gathers everything. Edwards began with the glory of God as the end for which the world was made. He spent his life on how that glory is seen, loved and lived. And he finished by asking Christians to pray, together and persistently, that the knowledge of that glory would fill the earth. He never saw the answer. He was dismissed by his congregation, exiled to the frontier, and died at fifty-four after five weeks in a post he had not wanted. By any ordinary measure his career ended in failure. The knowledge of the glory of the Lord is still spreading. He asked for that, and he is not here to see it, and it is happening anyway. That is generally how it works.

Be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord. 1 CORINTHIANS 15:58

One work, from beginning to end

Behind Edwards’s confidence in prayer lay a particular way of reading history, which he set out in a series of sermons preached at Northampton in 1739 and published afterwards as A History of the Work of Redemption. His thesis was that everything which has happened since the fall — every empire, every war, every migration, every obscure life — belongs to a single project, which is the redemption of a people for God through Christ. History is not a sequence of unrelated events with a religious thread running through part of it. The redemption is the plot, and everything else is the setting.

That in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth. EPHESIANS 1:10

He traced the work from the promise in Eden, through the flood, the calling of Abraham, the exodus, the monarchy, the exile, the prophets, to the incarnation — which he treated as the centre of the whole — and then onward through the spread of the gospel, to a consummation still ahead. The practical effect of reading history this way is considerable, and it is why this chapter belongs at the end of the book. It means that no faithful labour is isolated. The believer teaching six children in a village, the translator working through a difficult language, the congregation praying for a country closed to the gospel — each is contributing to a work that has been running for millennia and will certainly be completed. He is not starting something; he is joining something.

Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. PHILIPPIANS 1:6

It also supplies patience. Edwards’s own vantage point was a frontier village of a few hundred people, in a colony on the edge of the known world, at a moment when the gospel had reached a fraction of the earth. From there he wrote confidently about the knowledge of God filling the whole earth — not because the evidence around him warranted it, but because he had read what God said He would do.

So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please. ISAIAH 55:11

That is the ground of the concert of prayer. We are not asking God to attempt something. We are asking Him to hasten what He has already undertaken.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Join or begin a regular gathering whose explicit purpose is praying for revival and the spread of the gospel. Set a time and keep it. 2. Pray with believers outside your own tradition. Edwards’s proposal was deliberately across denominational lines. 3. Ask for something so large that you will not see it answered in your lifetime. Then keep asking. 4. Stop calculating timetables. Spend the energy on intercession instead. 5. Consider that the most fruitful thing you ever do may bear fruit after you are gone, and that you will probably not know. Work anyway.

A PRAYER
Lord of hosts, You have promised that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of Your glory as the waters cover the sea, and I have prayed as though You promised nothing of the kind.
Forgive the smallness of my asking.
Unite Your people in prayer across every line we have drawn between ourselves. Pour out Your Spirit. Advance Your kingdom in places I will never see, among people I will never meet.
I may not live to see the answer. Let me ask for it anyway, and labour, knowing that in You no labour is wasted. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory. 2 CORINTHIANS 3:18

Eighteen chapters can give the impression that Jonathan Edwards taught many things. He taught one thing, and everything else in him is an application of it. The one thing is this: God is infinitely glorious, the human problem is that we cannot see it, and salvation is God giving us eyes. Follow the chain and the whole system appears. God created the world for the display and communication of His glory. Human beings were made to see it, love it and reflect it. In the fall the capacity was lost — not the eyes but the taste, so that we look at what is supremely beautiful and feel nothing. That is why the will is bound: not because we are prevented, but because we do not want. Regeneration is the giving of a new spiritual sense, by which the same truths we always knew become suddenly lovely. From that new perception the affections move, and from the affections the whole life follows. And the end of the process is a world of love, where the seeing is unobstructed for ever. Justification, revival, the affections, true virtue, prayer — each is that one argument applied at a different point.

The danger of this book

If you have read this far, you are in a position of some hazard, and Edwards would have said so first. The peculiar risk of his theology is that it can be received as a system. It is a magnificent system, and a person can become an enthusiast for it — can learn to talk about the sense of the heart, the beauty of holiness, gracious affections — while remaining exactly the man he was, only better read. Edwards anticipated this precisely. It is why the final sign in Religious Affections is not an inward experience but Christian practice, and why he ranked it above everything a person might feel or remember. He knew that theological sophistication is one of the more effective disguises available to an unconverted heart.

But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. JAMES 1:22

So the plainest counsel this book can give is the same as before. Return to the chapter that made you least comfortable — not the one you found most interesting. Take its application points and work through them slowly over months. Then take the next.

What to carry away

Two things, if nothing else. First, ask for light. This is the request Edwards’s whole theology drives towards, and it is the one most of us never make. We ask God for help, for guidance, for provision, for comfort. We rarely ask Him to make us see that He is beautiful — which is the only request that changes anything at the root. You cannot argue yourself into loving God. You can ask.

Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law. PSALM 119:18

Second, watch your loves rather than your opinions. Edwards’s most useful gift to ordinary Christians is the shift of the diagnostic question from what do you believe? to what do you delight in? The second is far harder to answer dishonestly, and it is the truer map.

A last word about the man

We have been honest in these pages about his failures. He owned human beings while writing that virtue must extend beyond every private circle. He speculated about prophetic chronology and was wrong. He handled the crisis at Northampton in ways that cost him his ministry, and not all the fault lay with his congregation. He could be severe, and his severity did damage that his defenders have sometimes been too quick to explain away. None of that has been raised to diminish him. It has been raised because he, more than almost anyone, taught that the heart is deceitful beyond our capacity to detect, and that we are blindest where we most benefit. His life is the demonstration of his own doctrine. It would be a strange tribute to pretend otherwise. And there is this, which is the most hopeful thing in his whole story. The principle he failed to apply was applied by those who came after him, using his own arguments, against his own practice. The truth he taught outlived and overruled the man who taught it. That is what happens to true things. They do not depend on the vessel.

But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:7

Edwards died at fifty-four, five weeks into a job he had not wanted, in a town he barely knew, eight years after being dismissed by the congregation he had served for twenty-three. He was conscious near the end, and what he said to those around the bed was that they should trust in God, and then they need not fear. It is a small sentence for so large a mind. It is also, on his own principles, the only conclusion there was.

A PRAYER
Father, I have read about Your glory and I am not sure I have seen it.
I can describe the beauty of holiness and remain unmoved by it. I can explain the sense of the heart and not possess it. Do not let me settle for a theology of light without the light.
Open my eyes. Change what I love. And let the change show, not in what I can say, but in how I live when no one is watching.
You are glorious. Make me see it, and make me glad. Amen.

Take its application points and work through them slowly over months. Then take the next. What to carry away Two things, if nothing else. First, ask for light. This is the request Edwards’s whole theology drives towards, and it is the one most of us never make. We ask God for help, for guidance, for provision, for comfort. We rarely ask Him to make us see that He is beautiful — which is the only request that changes anything at the root. You cannot argue yourself into loving God. You can ask. Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law. PSALM 119:18 Second, watch your loves rather than your opinions. Edwards’s most useful gift to ordinary Christians is the shift of the diagnostic question from what do you believe? to what do you delight in? The second is far harder to answer dishonestly, and it is the truer map. A last word about the man We have been honest in these pages about his failures. He owned human beings while writing that virtue must extend beyond every private circle. He speculated about prophetic chronology and was wrong. He handled the crisis at Northampton in ways that cost him his ministry, and not all the fault lay with his congregation. He could be severe, and his severity did damage that his defenders have sometimes been too quick to explain away. None of that has been raised to diminish him. It has been raised because he, more than almost anyone, taught that the heart is deceitful beyond our capacity to detect, and that we are blindest where we most benefit. His life is the demonstration of his own doctrine. It would be a strange tribute to pretend otherwise. And there is this, which is the most hopeful thing in his whole story. The principle he failed to apply was applied by those who came after him, using his own arguments, against his own practice. The truth he taught outlived and overruled the man who taught it. That is what happens to true things. They do not depend on the vessel. But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:7 Edwards died at fifty-four, five weeks into a job he had not wanted, in a town he barely knew, eight years after being dismissed by the congregation he had served for twenty-three. He was conscious near the end, and what he said to those around the bed was that they should trust in God, and then they need not fear. It is a small sentence for so large a mind. It is also, on his own principles, the only conclusion there was. A PRAYER Father, I have read about Your glory and I am not sure I have seen it. I can describe the beauty of holiness and remain unmoved by it. I can explain the sense of the heart and not possess it. Do not let me settle for a theology of light without the light. Open my eyes. Change what I love. And let the change show, not in what I can say, but in how I live when no one is watching. You are glorious. Make me see it, and make me glad. Amen.

fields.title: A Reader’s Guide to Jonathan Edwards
fields.body_html:
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth. 2 TIMOTHY 2:15

Edwards is easier to obtain than almost any other major theologian and harder than most to read. Everything he wrote is out of copyright, and the complete Yale edition — twenty-six printed volumes, with a great deal more unpublished material — is available without charge from the Jonathan Edwards Center at Yale University. There is no financial barrier to reading him at all. The barrier is his prose. He wrote long, carefully qualified sentences for readers with more patience than we have. The remedy is to begin with the sermons, which were written to be heard, and to leave the treatises until the voice is familiar.

Begin here

A Divine and Supernatural Light (1734). Short, and the key to everything else. If you read one thing, read this. The Excellency of Christ. On the Lion and the Lamb. The most beautiful of his sermons and the most immediately accessible. Heaven is a World of Love, the closing sermon of Charity and Its Fruits (1738). The best correction to his reputation. Personal Narrative and the Resolutions. Brief autobiographical pieces, invaluable for seeing the man behind the arguments.

The central work

A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections (1746). His masterpiece and the basis of chapters eleven to fourteen of this book. It is long and demanding. Several reliable abridgements exist and there is no shame whatever in starting with one; the twelve signs in Part III are the heart of it and can be read on their own.

The major treatises

Freedom of the Will (1754). The most philosophically formidable thing he wrote, and hard going. Read a summary first. The Great Christian Doctrine of Original Sin Defended (1758). The End for Which God Created the World and The Nature of True Virtue, published together after his death as Two Dissertations (1765).

Short, dense, and the foundation of chapters one and fifteen.

On revival

A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God (1737). His account of the Northampton awakening; the book that made him internationally known. The Distinguishing Marks of a Work of the Spirit of God (1741). Brief and immediately useful for anyone assessing a movement today. Some Thoughts Concerning the Present Revival (1742). An Humble Attempt (1747). On united prayer. Skip the chronological speculation and keep the argument.

Also worth knowing

The Life of David Brainerd (1749). Edwards’s edition of the journals of the young missionary who died in his house. It became one of the most influential missionary books ever published, read by Carey, Martyn and Hudson Taylor. Read it aware that Brainerd’s relentless self-examination has harmed some readers as much as it has inspired others. A History of the Work of Redemption. Sermons tracing God’s single redemptive purpose through all of history.

About Edwards

George Marsden’s Jonathan Edwards: A Life (2003) is the standard modern biography and is outstanding — thorough, sympathetic and candid about the failures. Iain Murray’s Jonathan Edwards: A New Biography (1987) is warmer and more devotional, and less searching on the difficult matters. On slavery, the essential scholarship is by Kenneth Minkema, whose work brought the documentary evidence to light. Read more than one. No single account of him is disinterested.

Three counsels for reading him

Read him with the Bible open. His authority is entirely borrowed, and he would have been the first to insist that anything of his which cannot be sustained from Scripture should be discarded. Read him for the burden rather than the system. Where he presses a framework beyond what Scripture states — and in Freedom of the Will, in the mechanism of original sin, in the prophetic timetables, he does — take the pastoral concern and leave the scaffolding. Read him slowly, and aloud if the sentences resist. These are not books to be finished. A page a day, prayed over, will do more than a volume a week admired.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21
